Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email.

Just to clarify, our collections management system records items individually and does not group records together based on similar place names. We are not aware of any recorded information showing that records for Great House Farm, Llandough (near Cowbridge) or Great House Farm, Llandow were ever catalogued or treated within the collections system as relating to Great House Farm, Llandough (near Penarth/Cardiff).   The references to similarly named locations arose from our searches for information relevant to your request, rather than from any overlap within the collections records themselves.

In relation to item 7 of your email of 26 August, we do not hold any separate recorded information explaining the basis on which staff concluded that the identified records were unrelated to the reported nineteenth-century discovery. That conclusion was reached through staff assessment of the available records, and no further recorded information is held.

I hope this helps clarify our position.

Cofion cynnes,

Dear FOI Team,

FOI 2026-032

Diolch yn fawr. Thank you for the records, the descriptors and the published references. This is a thorough response and it is genuinely useful.

One correction of place is required.

The request concerns Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough near Penarth / Cardiff. Among the disclosed PAS material is at least one record for a different property of the same name: Great House Farm, Llandough near Cowbridge (including 2022.18.1, NGR SS9934672805, medieval lead Romanesque mount). There is also a Great House farm entry at Llandow. Those are not the site named in the request. Two Llandoughs, and more than one Great House Farm, sit in the same county. The homonym is easy to miss and material.

Please treat the Cowbridge / Llandow entries as out of scope for this request unless you hold recorded information showing they were, at any time, indexed, cited, or treated as if they related to Great House Farm, Llandough (Penarth / Cardiff). If any such cross-attribution exists in historic files, catalogues, correspondence, or search notes, that recorded information is within scope and I ask that it be disclosed.

If labels or findspot fields are now amended to distinguish the two farms, please do not overwrite the original wording without retaining the prior form. I ask that any correction be recorded as a dated amendment, with the earlier descriptor preserved, so the sequence of how the records stood when searches were first run remains inspectable. Please do not destroy, weed, or replace the versions as disclosed on 22 September 2026.

One small point from my email of 26 August also remains. As item 7 I asked for any recorded information showing the basis on which the Museum concluded that the identified records were unrelated to the reported nineteenth-century discovery. If that conclusion was reached by staff judgement and not written down, please simply confirm that no recorded information is held on that point. I am not asking for a new opinion.

Could you also confirm the date by which you expect to respond to FOI 2026-036?

Cofion,

Sion Buckler

Dear Hywel

Road closures will affect our community on the morning of Sunday 4th October for the Cardiff Half Marathon.

Penarth Road, Barry Road and Cogan Spur will all be closed, as the marathon course runs along these roads.

Llandough Hill will also be closed, to prevent vehicles diverted via Penlan Road from inadvertently trying to access Penarth Road while it's shut.
Diversions will be in place, and you can see the full road closure map above.

The closures will operate between 9am and 12pm.

Further details can be found at the Cardiff Half Marathon website here.  (https://www.cardiffhalfmarathon.co.uk/event-info/road-closures/)

https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1BzkRccTvm/

If you have further questions, Hywel, please let me know.


**
------------------------------------------------------------

Next community litter pick

Our last community litter pick has had great feedback.

I've even had a couple of messages asking when the next one is taking place!

Llandough Community Council organise these events throughout the year, but they usually put them on hold during the winter, due to lack of interest.

But given the enthusiasm, I thought it best to harness it!

We discussed it at last week's Community Council meeting, and I'm exploring organising another in the coming weeks.

I'll need to liaise with the Vale Council to arrange equipment, but the Community Council are on board and have said they'll help.

If you're interested in taking part, Hywel, drop me a message!
https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1KDWx1SUjX/

Licensing Service of
Revd Phil Maudsley

I had a wonderful evening on Tuesday at the Licensing Service of Reverend Phil Maudsley, the new Penarth Ministry Area lead.

It was great to see many members of our community there, including Llandough Community Council Chair Mo Misra, Reverend Susannah Griffin and lots of other residents.

Phil and his family have recently moved to South Wales from North Yorkshire, and I look forward to working with him.

I know everyone in Llandough will join me in welcoming them to our community.

Greenway Close verge

When I was out in our village recently, a Greenway Close resident raised the overgrowth on the nearby verge.

As you'll see from the first picture, it was in need of attention.

I raised with the Council. And I'm pleased to report it's now been cut back.

Thanks so much to the resident for coming over and raising this.

It helped ensure it was cleared.

As I always say, we're a team in Llandough.

By all chipping in, we make our village better for everyone.

If you ever spot anything that needs attention, Hywel, do let me know!

Preventing car thefts

I spoke with two people who've recently purchased Faraday boxes while I was out meeting residents this week.

With attempted car thefts reported in our village in recent months, police have advised everyone with keyless fobs to keep them in a Faraday pouch or box as a security measure.

It's a sensible precaution and a small expense to protect your car.

It was good to see people following the advice.

If you require further information, please drop me a message.

Community drop-in event:
20th October

Our next community drop-in event takes place at the Merrie Harrier on 20th October.

Like the last one, it'll start at 7.00pm.

The pub is a key asset to our community.

Tracey and the team do a lot for us - help return the favour by lending them your support.

You can see some of their midweek offers below!

https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EM9z5wbMs/

Sirs/Madam,

I write concerning the land now comprising Church View Close, Llandough,
formerly Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, including title WA231076 and former
title WA240304.

Persimmon Homes (Wales) Ltd is the current registered proprietor of
WA231076. Persimmon is therefore a present link in the conveyancing chain
arising from the registration of this land in BP Properties Ltd's name in
1982–83, BP's subsequent transfer to Ideal Homes in 1993, and the later
development history.

I am conducting a documented investigation into the legitimacy of that
title chain. This is not a speculative historical enquiry. The issues arise
from identified Land Registry, conveyancing, court, planning and
public-authority records, and from specific documentary gaps which remain
unresolved.

The central issue is the historic identity and ownership of the land.

The evidence presently assembled indicates two historically distinct
parcels:

• Parcel A: the farmhouse, garden, buildings, yard and associated woodland,
which the Williams family maintains was acquired out of the Bute estate
through the Daniel Thomas transaction and subsequently became the family's
freehold interest; and

• Parcel B: the eastern agricultural fields, whose subsequent passage from
Bute to Western Ground Rents and then to BP is not presently disputed by
the family.

The significance of that distinction is that later documents repeatedly use
the expression “whole farm”, although the surviving 1939 tenancy plan is
understood to show the eastern fields only. The 1938 Bute-to-Western Ground
Rents conveyance is therefore a material title-chain question: what estate
was actually capable of being conveyed by Bute in 1938, and did that
conveyance include Parcel A?

There is further evidence requiring examination of the period from 1949 to
1974, including repeated attempts to characterise Mary's occupation of the
farmhouse parcel as tenancy or permission; the loss of the family's title
papers in about 1950–52; the 1955 possession order expressed in “whole
farm” terms but enforced everywhere except the farmhouse and garden; the
separate 1962 possession proceedings concerning the farmhouse and garden;
Mary's express assertion of ownership; and the 1974 proceedings, which were
adjourned part-heard and were never finally adjudicated on the family's
historic ownership claim.

The Court of Appeal's decision in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA
Civ 2 subsequently concerned possession, limitation and the legal effect of
the October 1974 letters. The judgment records Mary's asserted ownership
and the absence of the documents she said supported it. The present
investigation therefore distinguishes carefully between what that judgment
decided concerning possession and limitation and the separate question of
whether the documentary root and extent of WGR/BP's title to Parcel A were
ever actually established.

That distinction becomes particularly important in relation to first
registration.

HM Land Registry records show BP's first-registration applications for
WA231076 and WA240304 in 1982–83. The surviving registration material also
identifies a 31 December 1969 conveyance from Western Ground Rents to BP
Pension Trust as a root of title, but that conveyance is not presently
included in the 30 July 2026 schedule of documents surviving on the
relevant first-registration files. The 1975 conveyance and plan, the
1982–83 registration material, the extent of the two titles and their later
amalgamation therefore require direct reconciliation against the underlying
documentary title.

There is also an unresolved procedural issue concerning notice and
opportunity to object during the 1982–83 first-registration process. Mary
Williams remained in occupation of the farmhouse. The family evidence
recorded on the evidence index is that notification was not received until
after her death on 26 March 1983. I am obtaining the primary notice,
service, application and registration records to establish exactly what
occurred.

The matters under investigation consequently include possible registration
mistake, procedural unfairness, material non-disclosure and, depending upon
what the primary records establish, possible fraud or deliberate
concealment. There are also unresolved public-authority record questions
involving HM Land Registry, court administration and other authorities.
These are identified as evidential questions, not asserted as established
findings against Persimmon or any individual.

Persimmon's position is therefore directly relevant because its present
registered title derives from the historic chain now being examined.

Please provide a substantive response to the following:

   1.

   *Title chain:* What documentary chain does Persimmon say establishes its
   predecessor's title to the whole of WA231076, including the farmhouse,
   garden and associated land now comprising Church View Close?
   2.

   *BP / Ideal Homes due diligence:* What title, acquisition and
   due-diligence documents were supplied to and reviewed by Persimmon in
   connection with the acquisition from Ideal Homes, including deeds, plans,
   title abstracts, searches, requisitions, Land Registry correspondence and
   enquiries concerning the extent of WA231076/WA240304?
   3.

   *Earlier title documents:* Does Persimmon hold, or has it ever held,
   copies of the 1969 WGR-to-BP Pension Trust conveyance, the 1975 BP Pension
   Trust-to-BP Properties conveyance and plan, the 1982–83 first-registration
   application/bundle, or documents explaining the inclusion of the farmhouse
   parcel within the registered extent?
   4.

   *1996 correspondence:* Does Persimmon retain the correspondence from
   March 1996 with HM Land Registry concerning WA231076, identified in the
   surviving title chronology as the last dealing on the file? If so, please
   provide a copy, subject to any properly applicable exemption or privilege.
   5.

   *Parcel A:* Has Persimmon ever reviewed the underlying documentary title
   sufficiently to satisfy itself that the farmhouse/garden parcel was
   actually comprised in the title acquired by BP, rather than being brought
   within the registered extent through the later “whole farm” description?
   6.

   *Present position:* Having regard to the matters above, does Persimmon
   maintain that its title to the farmhouse/garden parcel is supported by an
   identifiable documentary root independent of the possession and limitation
   history considered in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler?

If Persimmon maintains that the documentary title to Parcel A is
established, please identify the instrument or instruments on which that
position depends and the land those instruments actually comprise.

I am seeking voluntary or pre-action disclosure of non-privileged material
where possible. If any requested document is withheld, please identify the
document or category concerned and the basis upon which it is withheld.

*Preservation notice*

Please treat this correspondence as formal notice to preserve all documents
and electronically stored information within Persimmon's possession,
custody or control that may be relevant to the title, acquisition,
registration, extent, occupation, planning or development of this land.

This includes historical material inherited from BP Properties, Ideal Homes
or any other predecessor, together with deeds, conveyances, plans, title
abstracts, searches, due-diligence files, acquisition memoranda,
legal/property correspondence, Land Registry correspondence, planning
records and communications with public authorities.

Please ensure that no routine retention, deletion, destruction, disposal or
overwriting process removes potentially relevant material. This
preservation request includes electronic files, archived mailboxes and
other electronically stored information where applicable.

The public evidence index and supporting record are maintained at:

https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/

Nothing in this correspondence abandons, limits or prejudices any claim
concerning title, registration, fraud, deliberate concealment, procedural
unfairness, public-authority involvement, limitation, reopening of historic
proceedings, rectification/alteration of the register, compensation or
reparations. All rights and remedies are expressly reserved.

This correspondence is not a claim form and does not constitute service of
proceedings.

Please acknowledge receipt and refer this correspondence to Persimmon's
legal/property team. I request a substantive response addressing the
questions above.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant) Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare
Professional and Life Member

Freedom of Information / Data Management Team,

Request 719/26, and my request of 20 August 2026 (deaths of William Buckler
and Mary Doreen Williams)

1. Internal review of 719/26

I understand the Force's position is that it holds no records. I ask for an
internal review of that conclusion, because the search does not appear
capable of finding what the request describes.

South Wales Constabulary officers were present at the eviction and
demolition at Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, between 29 November
and 6 December 1988. This is not a matter of recollection. It appears in
ITV Wales footage from the time, now public on ITV's archive channel, and
in contemporary newspaper photographs and reports, which I can supply. A
police presence on that scale would have generated records: a duty or
deployment record, an operational order or briefing, an occurrence or
incident log, liaison with the Under-Sheriff or bailiffs, press office
material, and possibly photographs.

For the review, please confirm in writing:

(a) Which systems, archives and paper holdings were searched, including
pre-1990s paper records of the former Penarth/Barry division and any South
Glamorgan command records.
(b) The search terms used. Records of that period may be indexed under
"Leckwith Road", "Llandough", "BP Properties", "Buckler", "Williams", "Ty
Mawr", "eviction", "breach of the peace" or the date, rather than "Great
House Farm".
(c) Whether records of that type from 1988 were destroyed under a retention
schedule, and if so which schedule and whether any disposal record survives.
(d) Whether any records were transferred to Glamorgan Archives or the South
Wales Police Heritage Centre, with the reference if known.

If records were destroyed, a record of their destruction is itself
information I am asking for. If they are held elsewhere, please tell me
where, under your duty to advise and assist.

I was present at the eviction as a child. So far as any record contains my
personal data, please also treat this as a subject access request under
Article 15 UK GDPR.

2. Request of 20 August 2026

This request was due on 18 September 2026 and I have had no response beyond
the automatic acknowledgement. Please give me its reference and the
response. If the records are not held, please say whether they were
destroyed or passed to the Coroner.

If I do not receive the internal review outcome within 20 working days, I
will complain to the Information Commissioner.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Chief Executive / Complaints Officer,

This is a formal complaint to Heneb: The Trust for Welsh Archaeology, as
operational successor to the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust, and to
Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust Limited (The), company 01276976, which
remains an active company with its registered office at Heneb's address.

It concerns Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan (near
Penarth / Cardiff); ST 1681 7331; NPRN 20182. Cadw and RCAHMW have supplied
three unreconciled HER references for the same site: GGAT02038s, GGAT03586s
and GGATE003872.

This is not a chaser of my records request of 8 September 2026 or the
schedule of 19 September (ref GHF/HENEB/2026-09-20). That request remains
open and is due a response by 6 October. Please treat this complaint as a
separate file and give it a complaint reference.

What this is not. It is not an allegation that GGAT demolished the house,
advised that it be demolished, or decided that it should not be listed. It
is not an allegation of dishonesty, bad faith or criminal conduct. It is
not a title claim and I do not ask you to adjudicate BP v Buckler. GGAT's
letters of 13 and 15 December 1993, recommending a Breach of Condition
Notice when Condition 18 had not been met, were the Trust doing its
curatorial job. That is recorded here so it is not lost in what follows.

The charge, put narrowly. GGAT was the public curator of the regional
record; the adviser who told the planning authority it could not determine
89/01396/OUT without an archaeological assessment; the body which, in the
same document, specified machine-trench evaluation, quoted £2,000 and two
weeks, and recorded that it was already negotiating that work with BP
Properties; the contractor who then executed that evaluation on a
churchside monastic site its own 1978–80 excavations and its own 1982
letter had already flagged; and the author of a zoning map which treated as
empty ground in which, four years later, inhumations were found a few
centimetres below the topsoil. Disclosure of the dual role was not
management of it. The public record still does not reliably carry what was
found. Heneb's entire substantive reply since May is one sentence about
corporate form.

I enclose GGAT — Forensic Critique, Version 4.0.0 (21 September 2026). It
distinguishes established fact, reasonable inference, what cannot be
established, and facts that cut against the criticism. Where earlier
versions were wrong, the corrections are printed and kept. The critique is
the sourcing. This letter is the complaint. Please answer the letter. Treat
the critique as the schedule of sources, not as a substitute for numbered
answers.

1. I have not seen the HER

I do not assert the wording of GGAT02038s, because I have not been allowed
to read it. Cadw has said the content of the HER is managed by Heneb.
RCAHMW and Cadw have given three different identifiers for the same site.
Tests of Archwilio on 20 September 2026 did not return an error for
unresolved records. They returned a different record, from a different
trust, for a different site, with no warning:

GGAT02038s → GAT46242 (Gwynedd desk-based assessment)
GGAT03586s → GAT92911 (farmstead, Warwick Place, Gwynedd)
GGAT02038s, alternative path, three attempts → E001657 each time

A control query for an indexed record returned correctly. Please test those
three queries, correct the substitution if confirmed, and tell me the
outcome. Then permit inspection of the source file and supply an index of
every linked site and event record with its correct reference.

2. "Partially recorded" is RCAHMW's phrase, not a finding I have verified
on the HER

On 10 June 2026 Dr Adam Coward quoted NMR 6048945: "The house remained
partially recorded because of problems created by an ownership dispute. The
house and farm buildings were suddenly and completely destroyed by B. P.
Properties Ltd. on 6th December 1988 amid considerable local controversy."

That is the Royal Commission's file. I hold H. J. Thomas's measured
ground-floor plan of 26 April 1974, at 1:100, identifying the principal
rooms including the Dairy and recording the beams. GGAT reproduced that
plan as Figure 2 of its 1990 assessment, by kind permission. A measured
ground-floor survey that could not reach the first floor and roof is not,
without more, a failed survey.

Please state, from records you hold:
(a) whether the HER uses the phrase "partially recorded", and if so from
which source;
(b) what parts of the building the 1974 survey measured, and what it did
not;
(c) what contemporaneous document, if any beyond NMR 6048945, establishes
that access was restricted by the ownership dispute, by whom, on what date,
and to whom;
(d) whether Trench 7 of 1990 (north-east corner / former dairy, stone
floor, mortared partition) was ever reconciled against the 1974 plan, and
if the Trench 7 drawings, photographs and grid survive.

3. What GGAT held in 1988, and what it did not do

On 1 October 1982 GGAT told the Vale that occupation might continue north
of the church and that thorough investigative work should precede
development. Between that letter and November 1988 no GGAT act concerning
this site has been identified. RCAHMW added to its 1974 plan on 12 December
1988, six days after the demolition. There is no equivalent GGAT event. The
1990 report notes architectural features "observed in the rubble" and then
begins GGAT's own account with the words "Following the demolition… GGAT
entered into discussion with Debenham Tewson".

Please state what the SMR entry contained immediately before December 1988;
whether the 1982 advice was on it; whether any emergency building record,
watching brief on the demolition or the rubble, or post-demolition fabric
report exists; and where the carved stone and other architectural material
later referred to now is.

4. "County treasure"

GGAT 1989 §2.3: "At present our information on the Great House Farm area is
limited to the records of the recently demolished property which was listed
as a 'county treasure'." The phrase conferred no statutory protection.
Identify the list or card, the date, the criteria, and what information
about the building accompanied it. If you do not hold that document, say so.

5. Specify, price, bid, execute

In one 1989 consultee report GGAT advised that 89/01396/OUT should not be
determined without an assessment; specified machine-excavator trial
trenching; quoted two weeks at £2,000; and recorded that negotiations with
BP Properties via Debenham Tewson were already under way. BP then
commissioned GGAT. The 1990 report disclosed a "dual role" and invited
either party to go elsewhere. Disclosure is recorded. It is not the same as
management.

The IFA Code of approved practice for contractual arrangements was adopted
on 17 September 1990, after the assessment was delivered. It does not bind
that commission. The Welsh Archaeological Trusts' Code of Practice dates
from November 1997 and is not applied retrospectively. What did bind the
1989–90 arrangement, as contemporaneous standards rather than as a pleaded
cause of action: the IFA Code of Conduct in force from June 1985; the BADLG
Code, which GGAT expressly endorsed in the 1989 report; section 13 of the
Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982 as the implied standard of care
between GGAT and BP (the family was not a party); and the fiduciary duty of
charity trustees to identify and manage conflicts, not merely to notify two
commercial counterparties.

On 18 May 1994 GGAT's Curatorial Section wrote, of another contractor: "An
archaeological contractor should never be in the position of writing his
own Brief as well as carrying out the work." That principle was not met by
GGAT's own 1989–90 arrangement.

Please identify who wrote the 1989 recommendation, who accepted the
commission, whether those functions were separated, whether trustees or
Cadw were told, and who wrote the 1990 brief. If you hold Appendix "B" to
the officer's report (GGAT's further comments of 8 February 1990), Appendix
"D" (the representation from a County Councillor identified as a member of
GGAT), or Appendix "E" (the applicant's agents' written response to GGAT's
report), produce them. None of those three is in the planning file released
in 2026. Appendix "A" is. I do not assert that GGAT removed them. I ask
whether copies survive in GGAT/Heneb files.

6. The 1990 method against GGAT's own model

GGAT had excavated an early-medieval cemetery, a Roman villa and a
Tewkesbury Abbey grange immediately south of the same church, on the same
alkaline Liassic geology, and had written that occupation might continue
north of it. It chose eight machine-cut trenches, some placed "at random",
and then rated uninvestigated eastern ground "non existent to low"
potential. That rating converted a logistical limit into an empirical
claim. Cotswold's December 1994 preliminary report recorded that burials
continued into that zone and "lay only a few centimetres below the topsoil".

I do not say a 1990 evaluation had to predict 1,026 burials. I ask whether
the method was capable of detecting shallow inhumations on ground where
GGAT's own experience predicted excellent bone survival, and whether the
1990 evaluation has ever been reviewed against the 1994 results. If it has
not, will Heneb review it now.

7. Human remains and the 1981 Act

GGAT identified the Disused Burial Grounds (Amendment) Act 1981 and found
disarticulated human bone by the churchyard wall. That Act turns on whether
the land is a burial ground. A colour-coded potential map cannot answer it.
What legal advice was obtained, when, and from whom? What evidence set the
burial-ground boundary? Was a review undertaken after 1994?

8. Two burial figures, both correct

Cotswold's December 1994 preliminary report, §4.2: 858 inhumations and 152
disarticulated bone groups. Holbrook and Thomas, Medieval Archaeology 49
(2005): 1,026 burials comprising 814 articulated inhumations and 212
disarticulated bone groups, of which 801 skeletons received full
osteological analysis; "by far the largest Early-medieval burial population
so far recovered from Wales". They are the same excavation counted twice.
Please confirm which figure the HER now carries, and that both stages are
identified as such.

9. The c.1880 ironwork sentence, and what Amgueddfa Cymru now holds

GGAT 1990: "it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the
National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW
1988)." By 2005 that hedged sentence had become flat assertion in print.

Amgueddfa Cymru's disclosures of 25 August 2026 (FOI 2026-024 and internal
review 22 September 2026) and 22 September 2026 (FOI 2026-032) establish
the following, so far as the Museum holds recorded information:

(a) No accession, donation, transfer or deposit answering a visor, lance,
helmet, armour, soldier, horse, or nineteenth-century discovery under the
farmhouse floor.
(b) Accession 82.44H is the 1979 GGAT excavation assemblage. Collected by
Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust Ltd, 1979; donated 14 June 1982 by
Wales & West Housing Association Ltd; bibliographic reference Owen-John
1988. The collections database locality field is "Llandough Roman Villa",
NGR ST 168 733 — not "Great House Farm".
(c) Accession 95.56H is the 1994 Cotswold Archaeological Trust cemetery
assemblage. Collected by CAT, 1994; donated 28 July 1994 by Ideal Homes
Wales Ltd. Locality field: "Great House Farm Llandough", NGR ST 1681 7331.
Period on the human-remains entries: Early Medieval (c.400–c.1070).
(d) Accession 63.24 is objects stated to have been found at Church Farm,
Llandough, in 1858. The Museum's explanatory note of 22 September 2026
records that this is the only paperwork on that file, and that staff
consider it possible those objects are the basis of the later local story.
That is the Museum's observation, not a finding I ask you to adopt as fact.

Qualify or withdraw the 1880 sentence if you hold no source beyond the 1990
wording. Carry 82.44H and 95.56H on the principal HER description, with
collector, donor, donation date, locality field as catalogued, and NGR. If
the HER still points a professional user first to a post-medieval dwelling,
that is a record defect against what both excavations produced and what the
national museum now catalogues.

Please also confirm whether GGAT retained copies of the 1980 donation
correspondence with the National Museum (letters of 14 and 24 April 1980
are on the public record) and of any transfer file for 82.44H.

10. What the public record must now say

If GGAT02038s, or its successor identifier, still leads as a post-medieval
farm or dwelling, it does not satisfy the function of a working historic
environment record, and it is difficult to reconcile with section 194(2)(j)
of the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023. I have not seen the source
file, so I put that as a request for correction if the classification is as
described by Cadw officers, not as a finding I have verified on the face of
the record.

A professional user needs, in the principal description and not only in a
later narrative paragraph: the 1974 measured survey; GGAT's 1978–80 work
and 1982 advice; that the 1990 evaluation followed demolition and found
human bone; that the 1994 excavation recovered the assemblage above,
including in the 1990 low-potential zone; museum accessions 82.44H and
95.56H with their catalogued localities; and a note that the c.1880 NMW
ironwork attribution is uncorroborated by the institution said to hold the
object.

Please also reconcile the NGRs in use for the farmhouse, the 1990 trenches,
the 1994 excavation, the churchyard and the development parcels.
Distinguish this site from Great House Farm, Llandough near Cowbridge, and
from Llandow. Two Llandoughs sit in the same historic county. Homonym error
is a live records risk.

What I ask now

A. A complaint reference, the name of the person who will determine it, the
procedure you will apply, the timescale, and any independent review route.
Preserve all surviving Great House Farm records pending that determination.

B. Confirm which legal entity holds the records and functions formerly of
GGAT Ltd, and who handles HER corrections.

C. Answer sections 1 to 10 from the documents you hold. Where a document
does not survive, say when it left the file, under what retention rule, and
by whose authority.

D. Correct the HER so that the 1979 and 1994 investigations and accessions
82.44H and 95.56H sit in the principal description, the 1880 attribution is
qualified, the 1990 low-potential zone is annotated against the 1994
result, the three identifiers are reconciled, and Archwilio does not
silently substitute another trust's site.

E. Test and, if confirmed, correct the Archwilio substitution.

F. If you accept any part of this complaint, say what remedy you offer:
record correction, release of surviving files or an index, a written
account of the 1989–90 dual-role arrangement, and a methodological note on
the 1990 evaluation against the 1994 excavation.

I do not ask you to adjudicate title. I do ask you to account for what GGAT
knew, what it recorded, what it advised, what it then sold and executed,
what was found four years later, what the national museum now catalogues
from GGAT's own 1979 work, and whether the public record now tells the
truth of that sequence.

This letter is sent so that Heneb and GGAT Ltd have a fair opportunity to
investigate, answer, and offer remedy before any further process. Please
answer each numbered section. A general assurance that the organisation
acted appropriately will not do.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

conscious of that. I do travel back and forth to the UK and will visit
Leckwith in person, where I look forward to meeting you and the team and
thanking you personally.

I wanted to reply because I think I can now explain more precisely what I
am trying to establish from the records.

I am trying to reconstruct what happened historically which led my late
grandmother and father, over many decades, to continue asserting that our
family owned the land at Great House Farm, while that position was
repeatedly contested and ultimately possession was awarded to BP in *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler*.

What has caused me to revisit the documentary history is that the later
position is not as straightforward as I had previously assumed. Land
Registry has now told me that its position is not that it determined that
my family did not own the land; but it insists that no registration mistake
has been identified, which is what the MP forwarded me (they're fobbing him
off too).

Land registry will wake up to this soon I'm sure. Or I'm wrong and I need
to wake up. But I am a military warfare professional, and while I make
mistakes, or AI makes mistakes on my behalf, I have no issue holding my
hands up. I'm just trying to understand what happened to us and our home
and our land as children in the 80's, and why it all happened.

At the same time, I have so far found no convincing documentary evidence of
my family paying rent for the particular parcel which we occupied and
claimed as our own after the quarrying arrangement appears to have come to
an end.

I have therefore had one of my AI agents published my current
reconstruction, including the documentary sources behind it, here:

Great House Farm research <https://reference-url-citation.invalid/3>

I am not asking you to accept that reconstruction. It's clearly hit and
miss as an early technology. I am asking for your help in testing it
against the records held by Glamorgan Archives.
The central question

My present understanding is that what had originally been treated as one
agricultural holding can, when the surviving documents are examined
chronologically, be distinguished into two areas.

For simplicity, I have called them *Parcel A* and *Parcel B*:

   - *Parcel A* — the farmhouse, house plot, garden and associated land
   north/west of St Dochdwy's Church, occupied by my family; and
   - *Parcel B* — the agricultural land to the east which was subject to
   the agricultural tenancy and subsequently associated with Western Ground
   Rents.

I appreciate that “Parcel A” and “Parcel B” are my labels, not historical
descriptions appearing in the documents. But they aren't entirely just my
labels, parcel B is clearly what is in the 1939 map, which you hold, which
the council clerk for Llandough directed me to earlier this year, on his
day of retirement.

Also in 1983 two parcels were merged at the land registry, by BP. Which
confirms two parcels. I have purchased all those records avaliable and the
maps do confirm what I suspect.

The important question is whether the *underlying documents themselves
support the physical distinction*.

My working reconstruction is that the 1877 Daniel Thomas/Williams
arrangements ultimately resulted in my family acquiring the freehold
interest in the land around the farmhouse when the quarrying arrangement
came to an end, with the last machinery leaving in 1928.

If that is correct, it would explain something which otherwise appears very
difficult to reconcile.

The 1916 agricultural tenancy may have covered both parcels of the farm as
a whole at that time. But if part of that holding subsequently ceased to be
part of the agricultural tenancy because of my family's interest in the
parcel A crystallising into our freehold of parcel A, then the 1938 Western
Ground Rents acquisition and the *1939 revised agricultural tenancy* would
not necessarily concern our farmhouse land. Despite decades of it being
treated as though it did and our occupancy being allegedly permissive,
which is a narrative forced upon us to believe, when it most likely wasn't
the case. And why my nan rejected the premis and my dad too. Until their
dying breaths. I inherit this interest in this land parcel A as heir and
successor.

That is why the 1939 plan was so important and helpful.
The point I would particularly like you to confirm

*When you look at the actual 1939 Western Ground Rents revised tenancy and
its plan, I presume you see the same thing I see?*

My reading is that the plan depicts *Parcel B, the eastern agricultural
land, but does not depict or include Parcel A containing the farmhouse and
the land immediately associated with it.*

If that is what the plan shows, I would be very grateful if you could
simply confirm that.

If I am wrong, I would equally value you telling me that I am wrong and,
ideally, pointing me to the feature of the plan or accompanying document
which demonstrates that.

I am not asking you to determine what that means in law. Only whether *we
are looking at the same physical information in the same historical
document*.

That distinction is crucial because I am increasingly concerned that the
later history may have proceeded on the assumption that there was only one
undivided parcel, when the contemporary records may actually distinguish
two different interests.
I would like to do the same exercise with the other records

Your response itself says:

“With all historical research of this nature, it is necessary to piece
together information from surviving records that have been deposited with
us.”

That is precisely what I am now trying to do.

I understand the scientific process demands you look at the evidence and
tell what it tells. But I've done that, I'm making my case. And I'm
actually drawing the conclusion South Wales might be hexed under a spell
not seeing what I see. We also have hallucination with AI which is why I
ask for this specific clarification of the evidence you hold against my
interpretation of it.

Because in one hand I have the narrative, from court documents and news
articles saying we were squatters. In the other hand I have credible
evidence we had no issue relinquishing their parcel. The problem was all
with us on our parcel. And Western Ground Rents and BP don't appear to ever
had our parcel to be able to assert we were on it permissively. And the
1982 registration of their parcel in their name, is paradoxically based on
an alledged no contest our  occupancy was permissive. When its all we've
done since the 40's is challenge it. Almost a century.

I would therefore be grateful if, where reasonably possible, you could look
at the relevant surviving records and tell me whether the documentary
evidence supports, contradicts, or simply does not establish the following:

*1. 1916*

I think the 1916 agricultural tenancy appears to encompass the whole farm
as it then stood. Weather it was 2 seperate parcels then I don't know.

*2. 1877 / 1928*

Do the surviving Thomas/Williams/quarrying records support or contradict
the proposition that the farmhouse parcel was treated differently from the
eastern agricultural land, and that the relevant quarrying arrangement had
an effect on the family's interest in that land by 1928?

*3. 1938*

Does the Western Ground Rents conveyance or associated material show that
WGR acquired the farmhouse/house plot itself, or does it appear to concern
only the agricultural interest which subsequently appears in the 1939
tenancy?

*4. 1939*

Does the revised WGR tenancy plan contain only the eastern agricultural
parcel, excluding the farmhouse and its immediate land?

This is the point on which I would particularly appreciate a direct
confirmation or correction.

*5. 1955 / 1962 / 1974*

Do the surviving records contain any express documentary act which actually
transferred, extinguished or otherwise conclusively disposed of the
family's claimed interest in the farmhouse parcel?

I am deliberately not asking you to determine the legal effect of those
events. I am asking whether such an express documentary act appears in the
records.

*6. Later title history*

Do the surviving Glamorgan Archives records contain documentary evidence
showing how the farmhouse parcel itself passed from the earlier family
interest into Western Ground Rents, BP or another owner before the 1982/83
registration?

Or is that documentary chain simply not present in the surviving archive?
I would genuinely welcome correction

I want to emphasise this because I do not want this correspondence to
become an exercise in asking the Archive to validate my theory.

If I have misunderstood the records, *please tell me plainly*.

If the records support what I am seeing, please tell me that plainly too.

And if the surviving material cannot establish the point either way, that
is also a useful and perfectly acceptable answer.

Something as simple as:

*Supported by the surviving record*
*Not supported / contradicted by the surviving record*
*Cannot be determined from the surviving record*

would be enormously helpful to me, together with the relevant reference
where possible.

I am particularly keen to establish this because the research has already
demonstrated the value of going back to the underlying documents rather
than relying upon later descriptions of them. The 1877 material is a good
example: what initially appeared to be an inconsistency has been capable of
being reconsidered once the underlying research and records were examined.

That has made me realise that I need to make sure that I am not making the
same mistake in reverse.

I do not want to build an elaborate theory around a document which I have
simply misunderstood.
I am not asking the Archive to become a party to the dispute

I completely understand the distinction between an archive holding a record
and a court or Land Registry determining legal title.

I am not asking Glamorgan Archives to adjudicate the dispute, give me legal
advice, determine ownership, or take sides against any present landowner or
public authority.

I am asking for something considerably narrower:

*I want to know whether the historical documentary evidence held by the
Archive actually shows what I think it shows.*

That seems to me to be a legitimate research question for an archive
service, particularly where the answer can be expressed simply by reference
to what is physically depicted or expressly recorded in the documents.

I also appreciate that the statutory FOI duty itself does not necessarily
require an archive to create a new interpretation of information merely
because a requester asks for one. I am not trying to turn this into such a
demand. I am asking for professional assistance and dialogue in
understanding the historical material, which seems consistent with
Glamorgan Archives' own published access principles concerning open two-way
communication, active participation by users and responsiveness to the
community it serves. The wider Archive Service Accreditation framework
likewise recognises access and engagement with communities as a core part
of the function of an archive service.

I think that distinction is important.
Why this matters to me

I am trying to establish what actually happened to my late grandmother and
father's claimed ownership of their home and land.

My family maintained that claim for decades. The claim was contested. The
matter eventually resulted in the loss of possession and the subsequent
demolition of the farmhouse.

I completed 22 years of military service in 2024, leaving my career with
honour. I am now approaching this as a researcher trying to establish the
documentary truth of a family and community history.

I am not asking anyone to believe my family merely because it is our family
history.

Quite the opposite.

*I want the records to decide what can and cannot properly be said.*

That is why I would value an open exchange with the people who hold those
records.

If you look at the 1939 plan and say, “No, Sion, I don't think it excludes
the farmhouse parcel, and this is why,” I would consider that extremely
useful.

If you say, “Yes, I can see exactly what you are seeing — the plan depicts
the eastern agricultural land and does not include the farmhouse parcel,”
that is equally important.

And if the surviving records simply do not allow the point to be
determined, I would rather have that stated clearly than have either of us
infer something which the evidence cannot sustain.

I think that is the most constructive way for us to proceed.

There is a shared interest here in getting the history right. These are
records of the community in which we all live, and I think their greatest
value is realised when the surviving evidence can be examined openly,
critically and collaboratively.

I would therefore be very grateful if you could engage with the question at
that documentary level and tell me, as plainly as possible, *whether you
see what I see*.

Thank you again for all your assistance so far. I genuinely appreciate it.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

If you have made a request under the Freedom of Information Act or Environmental Information Regulations – the statutory timescale for response is 20 working days following receipt of your request.

If you have made a request in relation to your data rights, for example, a subject access request for personal data – the statutory timescale for response is one calendar month following receipt of your request.

Please note that where personal data is held on our register, it is exempt from the right of subject access under UK GDPR.

Where any personal data is held on record for a registered title, the exemption provided at Schedule 2, Part 1, Paragraph 5(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018 would be engaged.

“5(1) The listed GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

Yours sincerely

Information Rights Team
HM Land Registry

Accessing information held by HMLR on our register of title

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware most of the information held within our registers is open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we may be unable to provide access to this information via a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request.

Statutory Routes of Access to information held on Public Registers

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for keeping a register of title to land and property, and in accordance with Section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act, it is a requirement that the Chief Land Registrar makes this information (including any documents held on the register of title) available for public inspection.

How to access information held on our Registers

The information you have requested is available to access under our statutory protocol under section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act 2002.

Search for Land and Property

Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<http://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

Official Copies

For information about how to apply for official copies of documents held in relation to registered titles, and information about the types of documents available, please refer to practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Index of proprietors’ names

Under rule 11 of the Land Registration Rules 2003 the registrar is required to keep an index of proprietors’ names which shows for each individual register the proprietor of the registered estate and the proprietor of any registered charge together with the title number. When you search the index of proprietors’ names, you will receive a list of titles that are owned by, or mortgaged to, the name that you have searched against.

For further information about this please refer to practice guide 74:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names>

Section 21 FOIA exemption: Information accessible to the applicant by other means

Where information held on the register of title is available for inspection through these statutory routes of access it is exempt from disclosure under section 21(2)(b) of FOIA.

Section 21 states:

“21 Information accessible to applicant by other means.

(1) Information which is reasonably accessible to the applicant otherwise than under section 1 is exempt information.

(2) For the purposes of subsection (1)—

(a) information may be reasonably accessible to the applicant even though it is accessible only on payment, and

(b) information is to be taken to be reasonably accessible to the applicant if it is information which the public authority or any other person is obliged by or under any enactment to communicate (otherwise than by making the information available for inspection) to members of the public on request, whether free of charge or on payment.”

Therefore, we are unable to provide information held on our register through FOIA, as it covered by this exemption.

Advice and assistance

Under Section 16 of FOIA and in accordance with the Section 45 FOIA code of practice, we have a duty to provide you with reasonable advice and assistance.

Please note that the ICO has previously reviewed HM Land Registry’s use of the section 21 exemption. Relevant decision notices can be accessed here<https://icosearch.ico.org.uk/s/search.html?collection=ico-meta&profile=decisions&query&query=&f.By+authority%7CpublicAuthority=HM%20Land%20Registry&f.By+section%7CsectionOfLegislation=FOI%2021> including IC-173302-N4J1<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2022/4022883/ic-173302-n4j1.pdf>, FS50685812<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2017/2172810/fs50685812.pdf> and FER0454056<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2012/780474/fer_0454056.pdf>.

The ICO has agreed that this position is long established, and the Commissioner is satisfied that section 21 would be engaged for this type of request.

For assistance on how to obtain official copies of documents you can contact our Customer Support Centre by telephone between 8am and 5pm, Monday to Thursday on [phone redacted] or online through our Contact Us<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956> form.

If you need any support completing the application form for official copies or to determine which documents to order, you may contact our Customer Support colleagues:

www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>

You may also refer to our Publication Scheme which includes information about how to access information that is held on the register of title under the heading ‘Request information’:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information>

Please refer to HMLR’s Transaction Data webpage which contains information in respect of commonly used abbreviations:

www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data>

Please refer to the top tips:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information/>

Register information and your data protection rights

Data protection law permits HM Land Registry to use personal data for our official purposes.

The lawful basis for HM Land Registry processing personal data under the United Kingdom (UK) General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) is that it is necessary to enable us to perform our public task of the registration of land and property (Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR). This is defined in the Land Registration Act 2002.

Paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 Part 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018 provides the following exemption from the specified UK GDPR provisions:

“The listed UK GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for the keeping of a register of title to land and requirements for its administration by HM Land Registry under a Chief Land Registrar.

The Chief Land Registrar is required by the Land Registration Act 2002 and to make register information (including any documents held on the register of title) available to the public, therefore the following data protection provisions do not apply:


  *   the requirement to provide ‘privacy notices’ to individuals
  *   the requirement to provide personal data in response to subject access requests
  *   the requirement to rectification
  *   the requirement to comply with requests to erasure (right to be ‘forgotten’)
  *   most of the principles of UK GDPR

Sirs/ Ma'ams,

I need to correct a date I have used in earlier correspondence about Great
House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, titles WA231076 and WA240304.

I had treated 1983 as the year the two titles were merged. That was wrong.
HM Land Registry’s own letter of 23 March 2026 (Lisa Griffiths, ref
N610CGV) separates the two acts.
1982–83 was first registration of two live titles, not a merger.
30 November 1982: application to first-register WA231076. The Court of
Appeal later treated BP Properties Ltd as registered proprietors of “the
farm” from November 1982.
23 February 1983: application to first-register a second title, WA240304.
26 March 1983: Mary Williams died. On the family’s case, notice of those
applications did not reach us until after her death, while the family was
in mourning. She had no window in which to object. The family was not in a
position to use any window that arrived after that.
Those two titles remained separate through first instance.
24 July 1986: Hollis J. Both titles were still live. The judgment language
treats Great House Farm as one holding. It had not been one holding on the
register. On the family’s case it had not been one holding since the 1877
split: Parcel A (house, buildings, garden/yard and about 10 acres, the
Thomas/Williams line) and Parcel B (the eastern fields retained by Bute and
later WGR/BP).
2 February 1987: application to amalgamate the two titles. WA240304 was
then closed and registration continued under WA231076. That is the merge.
It was made after the 1986 ruling and before the Court of Appeal gave
judgment on 31 July 1987.
So 1983 is silent first registration of a second title while Mary was still
in Parcel A, or had only just died. 1987 is the administrative merger,
carried out while the appeal was still open.
This was not a dispute about a single land parcel that BP already owned.
Mary was on Parcel A, which the family says she owned, with occupation on
that house parcel running in the family from at least 1667. BP, and WGR
before it from 1949, were the neighbouring interest on Parcel B. From 1949
onwards the family’s case is that those neighbours ran a decades-long
series of tenancy offers, “whole farm” wording, possession orders and the
1974 letters to make her occupation of her own parcel look permissive, and
to make both parcels look like one estate they had acquired. They never
produced a conveyance of Parcel A. What they had was an unfounded claim
that her occupancy was permissive.
Please treat any earlier letter from me that said the titles merged in 1983
as corrected by this email. The dates that matter are:
1982/83 — first registration of two titles, without the occupier being
heard;
24 July 1986 — first-instance judgment describing one farm while two titles
still stood;
2 February 1987 — amalgamation, before the appeal ended;
31 July 1987 — Court of Appeal.
Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler
Refs where relevant: N610CGV; 260919-6726246; titles WA231076 and WA240304.

Dear Sirs,

I am seeking an independent review of HM Land Registry's handling of my
complaint concerning the historic registration of land belonging to the
Williams/Buckler family at Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, Cardiff,
and the subsequent registered title history, including WA231076, WA240304
and the later woodland title WA735527.

HM Land Registry has now replied to my MP and has maintained, in essence,
that it does not accept that a mistake was made.

My concern is not simply that HM Land Registry reached a conclusion with
which I disagree. It is that the conclusion appears to leave fundamental
documentary questions unanswered and relies heavily upon historical
proceedings which did not determine the underlying documentary root of the
family's ownership claim.

I have spent approximately twenty years researching this matter and have
assembled a substantial body of documentary, archival, court, Land Registry
and family evidence. I am not asking ICR to determine ownership itself. I
am asking it to review whether HM Land Registry properly investigated and
answered the complaint put before it, whether it addressed the evidence I
supplied, and whether the reasons given for its conclusion adequately
explain how the disputed registration was accepted and subsequently
maintained.
1. The underlying family ownership claim

The family's position is that our historic Parcel A was a distinct parcel
of land around the farmhouse and woodland and that our underlying freehold
interest was never lawfully extinguished.

My grandmother, Mary Williams, consistently asserted ownership of the
family parcel. The documentary history presently available to me raises a
substantial question as to whether Parcel A was ever conveyed to Western
Ground Rents in the manner subsequently assumed.

There is an important distinction between:

   - the family-occupied Parcel A surrounding the farmhouse; and
   - the eastern agricultural Parcel B which was the subject of the later
   agricultural tenancy arrangements.

The 1939 revised agricultural tenancy documentation which I have located
appears to concern Parcel B and its associated land. The accompanying plan
does not appear to include the family-occupied Parcel A.

This raises a basic documentary question:

What instrument actually conveyed Parcel A to Western Ground Rents, if it
was ever conveyed to them at all?

I have not yet obtained a document which satisfactorily answers that
question.
2. The 1928 / 1938 / 1939 documentary sequence

The present reconstruction begins with the 1877 arrangements involving the
Marquess of Bute and Daniel Thomas & Son and the subsequent quarrying
arrangements.

My understanding from the evidence presently assembled is that the relevant
quarrying arrangements were completed by 1928 and that the family
thereafter continued in occupation of Parcel A as its own land.

The later 1938 conveyancing from the Bute estate to Western Ground Rents
therefore requires close examination as to precisely what land was conveyed.

This is particularly important because the 1939 revised agricultural
tenancy record naming Western Ground Rents as landlord appears, from its
plan, to concern Parcel B rather than Parcel A.

That record was brought to my attention by the clerk for Llandough Town,
who directed me to the archive material shortly before his retirement
earlier this year.

If Parcel A was not conveyed to Western Ground Rents in 1938, and was not
included in the 1939 agricultural tenancy, the subsequent legal narrative
by which the family's occupation came to be treated as permissive requires
considerably more examination than HM Land Registry's present response
appears to have given it.
3. The successive attempts to characterise the family occupation as
permissive

The historical evidence reveals a sequence of events which I believe needs
to be examined as a whole rather than in isolation.

These include:

*1949* — an attempted tenancy arrangement concerning Parcel B which appears
to have sought to include my grandmother in the tenancy and thereby connect
her occupation of Parcel A with the agricultural tenancy of Parcel B;

*1951* — the disappearance of important family papers, including the
family's title documentation, which my grandmother reported as stolen;

*1955* — possession proceedings in which the language concerning the “whole
farm” requires comparison with the actual definition of the agricultural
holding and its separate parcels. The order also expressly excluded the
“house and garden” and referred to my grandmother's “condition and
resistance”;

*1959* — an offer of a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden, which my
grandmother rejected while continuing to assert an ownership claim;

*1962* — a possession order concerning the farmhouse and garden, the legal
effect and subsequent enforcement history of which require examination;

*1965* — a further attempt to place “Mrs Williams” into a weekly tenancy,
again rejected;

*1974* — an ownership action was adjourned; leave to enforce the 1962
possession order was obtained but the warrant was not pursued; and BP
subsequently relied upon the two letters of 31 October 1974 as establishing
a licence relationship.

The family interpretation is that these were not independent, isolated
events but a succession of attempts to convert or present an allegedly
proprietary occupation as permissive.

I appreciate that this is an interpretation requiring documentary testing.
That is precisely why I believe HM Land Registry should have engaged with
the underlying documents rather than treating the later registered position
and the 1987 Court of Appeal judgment as effectively resolving the matter.
4. The 1987 judgment does not answer the documentary provenance question

A particularly important part of my complaint concerns the way HM Land
Registry has relied upon *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* [1987] EWCA Civ 2.

I do not dispute that this was an important Court of Appeal decision.

However, the case concerned the adverse-possession and possession issues
concerning the farmhouse and garden. The Court considered the
registered/paper-title position relied upon by BP, the previous possession
proceedings and the legal effect of the 1974 letters upon the character of
Mrs Buckler's occupation.

The judgment itself records that Mary Williams had asserted that she had a
title to Great House Farm through her grandfather and believed that
documents existed establishing that title, but that such documents were not
produced.

The point is therefore not that the Court of Appeal “never touched title”.
It plainly considered BP's registered/paper-title position.

The point is narrower and, in my view, fundamental:

The 1987 judgment is not itself the conveyance, plan, root deed or other
documentary instrument establishing how the woodland and the family's
historic Parcel A entered BP's registered title.

Nor did it adjudicate the validity of Forest of Cardiff's separate 1994
acquisition of the woodland.

I am concerned that HM Land Registry's present response treats the 1987
judgment as though it answers a documentary provenance question which it
did not determine.
5. The 1969 conveyance and 1971 abstract

HM Land Registry has also told me that BP supplied a title chain extending
back to 1969.

That raises another substantial documentary issue.

There were only thirteen years between the 1969 conveyance and BP's first
registration in 1982.

The 1969 conveyance from Western Ground Rents to BP Pension Trust therefore
requires examination as to exactly what proprietary interest was being
conveyed.

I understand the later title documentation to recite the 1969 conveyance as
a root document, while the 1971 abstract refers to the 1962 possession
order and an OS plan.

If the underlying title to Parcel A was never conveyed to Western Ground
Rents, the critical question is how an asserted interest arising from
possession proceedings could subsequently be treated as though it were
documentary title to the parcel itself.

The 1971 abstract is therefore particularly important.

HM Land Registry's own correspondence has recorded that such an abstract
was lodged. The 30 July 2026 schedule of surviving first-registration
documents does not identify the 31 December 1969 conveyance itself, nor
does it resolve the evidential gap concerning the 1971 abstract.

I am continuing to pursue those underlying records.
6. The 1982–83 registrations

My principal concern is that BP may have registered not the family's actual
historic Parcel A, supported by a lawful root title, but a later
constructed or “synthetic” parcel derived from the succession of
possession, tenancy and licence documents which had been used to
characterise the family occupation as permissive.

I use “synthetic parcel” as a description of the issue I am investigating,
not as a statement that this is already legally established.

The essential question is:

What precise land did BP apply to register in 1982–83, what documentary
instrument entitled BP to register that land, and did that land correspond
to the land actually conveyed to BP's predecessors?

The later amalgamation of the BP titles is also significant because what
may have originated as separate parcels or interests appears subsequently
to have been brought together within the registered estate.

It is necessary to establish whether that process merely recorded an
existing lawful title or whether it caused an underlying proprietary
boundary to disappear within a later registered estate.
7. HM Land Registry's response

HM Land Registry has now maintained that it was correct to register the
land and has relied, in part, upon the 1987 judgment.

I respectfully submit that this does not answer the complaint.

An administrative conclusion that a registration was “correct” cannot
itself reconstruct a missing conveyance, establish the precise boundary of
land conveyed decades earlier, or demonstrate that a later registered
proprietor had documentary title to a distinct parcel where the underlying
conveyancing remains disputed.

Nor does the existence of the 1987 judgment establish the documentary
provenance of WA735527 or the validity of the separate 1994 transfer to
Forest of Cardiff.

I am particularly concerned that HM Land Registry appears to regard its
reliance upon the 1987 judgment as effectively validating the 1982–83
registration, when the registration itself pre-dated the judgment.

The chronology matters.

The registration came first.

The litigation came afterwards.

I therefore cannot see how a later judgment concerning possession and
adverse possession can, without further analysis, resolve whether the
earlier registration accurately represented the documentary title existing
at the date of registration.
8. Notification and my grandmother's death

Another issue which requires consideration is notification.

To my knowledge, the family was not notified that BP had applied to
register the relevant land in 1982.

My grandmother died on 14 March 1983, shortly after the first registration
and within the period in which the registration would have been capable of
being challenged had she known of it.

She had spent decades rejecting attempts to characterise her occupation as
permissive and consistently maintaining an ownership claim.

The fact that she died shortly after the registration is not itself proof
of wrongdoing. It is, however, a material chronological fact when
considering whether she had a meaningful opportunity to challenge the
registration and whether HM Land Registry appropriately considered the
notification history.

I ask the ICR to consider whether HM Land Registry has adequately addressed:

   - what notice was given of the 1982 application;
   - to whom it was given;
   - what information was supplied to the persons potentially affected;
   - whether any competing ownership claim was disclosed by the applicant;
   - and what records exist showing how HM Land Registry assessed those
   matters.

9. Possible fraud, concealment and institutional involvement

Through my research I have also identified matters which I consider may
warrant investigation for possible fraud, deliberate concealment,
misrepresentation, mistake and institutional involvement.

I want to be precise about this.

I am not asking the ICR to find that fraud occurred.

I am asking the ICR to consider whether HM Land Registry adequately
investigated evidence raising those questions, particularly where the
evidence concerns missing historic documents, the distinction between
Parcel A and Parcel B, the provenance of the 1969 title, the 1971 abstract,
the 1982–83 registrations and the subsequent amalgamation of titles.

I have deliberately distinguished established documentary facts from
matters which remain hypotheses requiring investigation.

There are also serious questions concerning the destruction or absence of
historical records and the later treatment of the land. Those matters are
being pursued through separate archival and documentary channels.
10. The human and public-interest dimension

This is not merely an abstract registration dispute.

My grandmother was a disabled widow and amputee who maintained an ownership
claim to the family land through decades of litigation and repeated
attempts to characterise her occupation as permissive.

The family was ultimately removed from the property in 1988. The historic
farmhouse, which had been our family home and which we believe had
significant architectural and historic importance, was subsequently
demolished.

I was a child when we were removed.

Family possessions and historic material were lost or dispersed, while the
land was subsequently developed and altered.

The family's connection with the site is recorded as extending back to the
seventeenth century, and I was born at Great House Farm.

There are also wider heritage and archaeological questions concerning the
site and its subsequent development, which I am investigating separately.

I mention these matters because they explain why I have continued the
investigation for approximately twenty years and why the accuracy of the
underlying land record matters so profoundly to my family.

My professional background is in military cyber and electronic warfare, and
much of my research has involved reconstructing fragmented documentary
histories and identifying discrepancies between records. I have approached
this as an evidential investigation rather than simply as a family
grievance.
11. Why I am approaching the ICR

I therefore ask the ICR to review HM Land Registry's handling of my
complaint and, in particular, whether it:

   1.

   adequately investigated the distinction between historic Parcel A and
   Parcel B;
   2.

   adequately considered the 1938 conveyance and 1939 revised tenancy plan;
   3.

   adequately addressed the documentary provenance of the 1969 conveyance
   and the 1971 abstract;
   4.

   adequately examined the precise land comprised in the 1982–83
   registration applications;
   5.

   relied upon the 1987 *BP v Buckler* judgment for a proposition which the
   judgment itself did not determine;
   6.

   adequately considered the chronology whereby the 1982–83 registration
   preceded the 1987 judgment;
   7.

   adequately investigated the notification given to persons asserting
   ownership of the land;
   8.

   adequately addressed the missing or unavailable historic documents and
   the evidential gaps I have identified;
   9.

   adequately considered the evidence I supplied rather than simply
   reaffirming the existing registered position; and
   10.

   provided reasons sufficient to explain why, notwithstanding those
   unresolved documentary questions, HM Land Registry considers that no
   mistake or registration error occurred.

I am not asking the ICR to adjudicate the family's ultimate title claim.

I am asking for an independent examination of whether HM Land Registry's
investigation and reasoning were adequate, proportionate and properly
responsive to the evidence and issues actually raised.
12. Documents and evidence

I can provide the relevant correspondence with HM Land Registry, the
response to my MP, registration material, historical conveyancing, court
records, archival plans, family evidence and other documents relied upon in
my complaint.

I also maintain a detailed chronology of the matter, including:

1916 — agricultural tenancy;

1928 — completion of the relevant quarrying arrangements;

1938 — Bute / Western Ground Rents conveyancing;

1939 — revised agricultural tenancy and plan;

1949 — tenancy attempt;

1951 — missing/stolen title documentation issue;

1955 — possession proceedings;

1959 — farmhouse and garden tenancy offer;

1962 — possession order;

1965 — further tenancy attempt;

1969 — Western Ground Rents → BP Pension Trust conveyance;

1971 — abstract and plan material;

1974 — ownership proceedings, possession enforcement history and licence
letters;

1975 — BP Pension Trust → BP Properties transfer;

1982 — first registration;

1983 — subsequent registration and title dealings;

1987 — *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* Court of Appeal judgment;

1988 — final removal from the farmhouse and demolition; and

1994 — subsequent acquisition of the woodland by Forest of Cardiff.

The chronology is significant because it demonstrates why I do not consider
the 1987 judgment, standing alone, capable of answering the earlier
registration question.
13. What I am asking for

I respectfully ask the ICR to accept this as a request for independent
review of HM Land Registry's handling of the complaint.

In particular, I ask that the reviewer consider whether HM Land Registry
has actually answered the documentary questions raised, rather than merely
reaffirming the registered position.

I would also ask that the underlying Land Registry records relevant to the
1982–83 registration, notification, supporting title documents, plans, the
1969 conveyance and the 1971 abstract be considered where they remain
available.

I am not seeking a finding against individual Land Registry staff.

I am seeking an independent assessment of whether the institution's
handling of this matter has been adequate and whether the reasons given for
refusing to recognise a possible mistake are properly supported by the
underlying record.

The issue remains live because the disputed land is now being dealt with
through subsequent titles and, in the case of the woodland, is presently
subject to a proposed disposal by Forest of Cardiff.

I therefore respectfully ask the ICR to consider this matter on the basis
of the documentary chronology and evidence rather than treating the
existence of the current register as dispositive of the historical question.

I am willing to provide a structured evidence bundle and chronology to
assist the review.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

   catalogue metadata on Discovery, rather than the date on which the physical
   records entered TNA custody.

Your response states:

“The initial response from our records enquiries team looked for the four
