Mr Wigley,
I am writing to make a formal complaint to Cadw concerning the handling and substantive response to my correspondence regarding Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, and particularly Cadw's 1988 consideration of whether the building should
 be protected by listing.
I am making this complaint directly to Cadw at this stage because I consider that Cadw should be given a proper opportunity to review and address the matters before any escalation to the wider Welsh Government complaints process.
For the avoidance of doubt, I am not making a further Freedom of Information request and I am not simply asking Cadw to produce records which it has already said no longer exist. I accept that Cadw has stated that all records it currently
 holds concerning the 1988 listing decision have been released.
My complaint concerns what can properly be established from the surviving evidence, whether the responses I have received have adequately addressed that evidence, and whether the historical record can now be described accurately where the underlying file
 has been lost.
1. The newly identified 1982 evidence
I have now identified a 1 October 1982 consultation letter from the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust concerning the East Vale Local Plan and the proposed Ty Maw Farm site, identified as
H2.1.
The letter states:

“Ty Maw Farm (H2.1) is designated as a three-acre residential site. As you will see from the enclosed information the settlement at Llandough developed considerably from farming and fishing... Recent excavations at Llandough by the Trust revealed early occupation,
 part of the villa and medieval grange buildings. There remains a possibility that occupation continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore, for thorough investigative work prior to the development.”

I do not suggest that this document, by itself, establishes that the standing farmhouse was required to be listed.
Its significance is narrower and more demonstrable: six years before the 1988 demolition, the archaeological and planning system already contained site-specific information identifying Ty Maw Farm as a proposed development site and recording substantial
 archaeological sensitivity in the immediate Llandough area, including possible continued occupation north of the church.
That materially affects the historical context in which Cadw's 1988 assessment needs to be understood.
I therefore ask Cadw to address:


Whether this 1982 information was held by, available to, or capable of being obtained by Cadw in the period leading to the 1988 decision.

Whether Cadw has any surviving evidence showing what archaeological, planning or historic-building information was available to the inspectors or decision-makers in 1988.

Whether there was communication between Cadw and the relevant planning/archaeological authorities concerning the proposed development of Ty Maw Farm and the need for investigation or protection.

If it is no longer possible to establish whether this evidence was actually considered, whether Cadw will expressly acknowledge that uncertainty rather than treating the absence of the historic file as evidence that the relevant information was absent.

2. The 1974 RCAHMW survey
I have previously drawn Cadw's attention to the 26 April 1974 Royal Commission survey by H.J. Thomas at ST16817331.
That survey recorded Great House Farm as a historic building, including features such as the late seventeenth-century character of the house, its cross-passage arrangement, adze-worked beams, ogee stops and barrel-vaulted cellar.
Cadw has stated that only two photographs from its relevant historic material survive and that it cannot now establish whether the 1974 survey was taken into account in the 1988 listing consideration.
I accept that this may now be incapable of being proved from the surviving file.
However, there is an important distinction between:
“Cadw cannot now establish whether the information was considered”
and
“there is no evidence that the information was available or relevant.”
The surviving RCAHMW material demonstrates that professional historic-building recording existed well before the 1988 decision.
I therefore ask Cadw to address specifically whether that material was available to Cadw through the inter-agency heritage system at the time and, if so, what can now be established about its availability.
3. Cadw's own evidence that listing was actively being considered in 1988
The surviving contemporary material indicates that in December 1988 Cadw was actively considering emergency protection/spot-listing of Great House Farm, including inspection and consultation concerning the building's historic significance.
That is important because it demonstrates that this was not retrospectively invented as a heritage issue decades later. Cadw itself was considering protection immediately before the building was demolished.
Cadw's present position is that the historical listing file no longer survives and that its retention arrangements at the time cannot now be established with certainty.
I am not asking Cadw to speculate about what a destroyed file contained.
I am asking Cadw to distinguish clearly between:

what the surviving evidence positively establishes;what information was demonstrably available by 1988;what actions by Cadw in 1988 can still be established;what cannot now be established because the historic record has been lost; andany conclusions Cadw considers cannot responsibly be drawn.
That distinction is particularly important when assessing whether the surviving record provides a sufficiently reliable account of what happened.
4. The planning authority and temporary protection
I also wish to clarify the position concerning temporary protection.
I am not suggesting that Cadw itself necessarily possessed the statutory power to serve a Building Preservation Notice. I understand that such protection was a matter for the relevant local planning authority under the legislation then in force.
The question for Cadw is therefore whether, during the 1988 consideration, 
Cadw advised, discussed or communicated with the relevant planning authority concerning any available temporary protection mechanism or the need to prevent demolition pending consideration of listing.
If Cadw cannot establish what was discussed because the records no longer survive, that should be stated expressly.
5. The later description of Great House Farm as “a listed building”
I have also identified later archaeological/planning documentation in which the former site is described in terms including:

“The site formerly contained Great House Farm (a listed building).”

I am not asserting that this wording conclusively proves that Great House Farm was formally listed at that time.
I am asking Cadw to explain, insofar as the surviving evidence permits, whether there is any known provenance for that description and whether Cadw considers it accurate, erroneous, or simply impossible now to determine.
This is relevant because it illustrates the existence of potentially conflicting historical accounts concerning the building's protection status.
6. The significance of the loss of the 1988 record
Cadw has understandably stated that the historic file cannot now be produced.
However, the loss of that file creates a historical evidential limitation; it should not automatically resolve questions arising from the surviving evidence in Cadw's favour.
The appropriate conclusion may simply be that some aspects of the 1988 decision
cannot now be reconstructed with certainty.
I would therefore like Cadw to consider whether its previous responses have drawn that distinction sufficiently clearly.
7. What I am asking Cadw to do
I am asking Cadw to treat this as a formal complaint and provide a substantive response addressing the following:
A. Whether the newly identified 1982 GGAT evidence materially changes Cadw's understanding of the information environment surrounding Ty Maw Farm before the 1988 demolition.
B. Whether Cadw can establish that the 1974 RCAHMW survey was available to it in 1988.
C. Whether Cadw can establish what archaeological, planning and historic-building information was available to its officers when the building was being considered for protection.
D. What can now be established about Cadw's communications with the local planning authority and other heritage bodies during the 1988 listing consideration.
E. Whether temporary protection was discussed or advised upon and, if not capable of being established, whether Cadw will state that plainly.
F. What can be established about the inspection of Great House Farm and the ultimate listing decision.
G. Whether Cadw accepts that the loss of the historic file means that some aspects of the 1988 decision can no longer be reconstructed reliably.
H. Whether Cadw considers the surviving documentary evidence, including the 1974 survey and 1982 archaeological/planning evidence, should be reflected in any relevant contemporary heritage record or historical account.
I. Whether Cadw can explain the provenance, insofar as it is capable of doing so, of the later description of the former site as containing “a listed building.”
J. Whether Cadw considers that its previous responses have adequately distinguished between the absence of surviving evidence and evidence that something did not happen.
8. Scope of this complaint
I want to be clear that I am not asking Cadw to determine my family's wider property or title claims, nor am I asking Cadw to reach a predetermined conclusion about the historical ownership of the land.
Those matters are separate.
This complaint is confined to Cadw's own heritage-related role, the 1988 protection/listing process, the information that can now be established as having existed, and the adequacy and accuracy of Cadw's present explanation of that history.
I am also not asking Cadw to speculate about missing documents. On the contrary, I ask that the absence of those documents be treated as an evidential limitation and expressly identified as such.
9. Requested outcome
I would like Cadw to:


Register this as a formal complaint and provide a complaint reference.

Have the matter reviewed by an appropriate person who has not simply repeated the previous FOI position.

Provide a point-by-point response to the matters above, taking account of the newly identified 1982 evidence.

Correct or clarify any part of Cadw's previous correspondence that is found to have been incomplete, inaccurate or insufficiently qualified.

State clearly which matters can now be established, which cannot, and which remain uncertain because the historical records no longer survive.

I regard that as a proportionate and reasonable opportunity for Cadw to address the matter directly before I consider whether escalation through the Welsh Government complaints process is necessary.
Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Mr Wigley,

I am writing to make a *formal complaint to Cadw* concerning the handling
and substantive response to my correspondence regarding Great House Farm
(Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, and particularly Cadw's 1988 consideration of whether
the building should be protected by listing.

I am making this complaint directly to Cadw at this stage because I
consider that Cadw should be given a proper opportunity to review and
address the matters before any escalation to the wider Welsh Government
complaints process.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am *not making a further Freedom of
Information request* and I am not simply asking Cadw to produce records
which it has already said no longer exist. I accept that Cadw has stated
that all records it currently holds concerning the 1988 listing decision
have been released.

My complaint concerns what can properly be established from the surviving
evidence, whether the responses I have received have adequately addressed
that evidence, and whether the historical record can now be described
accurately where the underlying file has been lost.
1. The newly identified 1982 evidence

I have now identified a 1 October 1982 consultation letter from the
Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust concerning the East Vale Local Plan
and the proposed Ty Maw Farm site, identified as *H2.1*.

The letter states:

“Ty Maw Farm (H2.1) is designated as a three-acre residential site. As you
will see from the enclosed information the settlement at Llandough
developed considerably from farming and fishing... Recent excavations at
Llandough by the Trust revealed early occupation, part of the villa and
medieval grange buildings. There remains a possibility that occupation
continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore,
for thorough investigative work prior to the development.”

I do not suggest that this document, by itself, establishes that the
standing farmhouse was required to be listed.

Its significance is narrower and more demonstrable: *six years before the
1988 demolition, the archaeological and planning system already contained
site-specific information identifying Ty Maw Farm as a proposed development
site and recording substantial archaeological sensitivity in the immediate
Llandough area, including possible continued occupation north of the
church.*

That materially affects the historical context in which Cadw's 1988
assessment needs to be understood.

I therefore ask Cadw to address:

   1.

   Whether this 1982 information was held by, available to, or capable of
   being obtained by Cadw in the period leading to the 1988 decision.
   2.

   Whether Cadw has any surviving evidence showing what archaeological,
   planning or historic-building information was available to the inspectors
   or decision-makers in 1988.
   3.

   Whether there was communication between Cadw and the relevant
   planning/archaeological authorities concerning the proposed development of
   Ty Maw Farm and the need for investigation or protection.
   4.

   If it is no longer possible to establish whether this evidence was
   actually considered, whether Cadw will expressly acknowledge that
   uncertainty rather than treating the absence of the historic file as
   evidence that the relevant information was absent.

2. The 1974 RCAHMW survey

I have previously drawn Cadw's attention to the 26 April 1974 Royal
Commission survey by H.J. Thomas at ST16817331.

That survey recorded Great House Farm as a historic building, including
features such as the late seventeenth-century character of the house, its
cross-passage arrangement, adze-worked beams, ogee stops and barrel-vaulted
cellar.

Cadw has stated that only two photographs from its relevant historic
material survive and that it cannot now establish whether the 1974 survey
was taken into account in the 1988 listing consideration.

I accept that this may now be incapable of being proved from the surviving
file.

However, there is an important distinction between:

*“Cadw cannot now establish whether the information was considered”*

and

*“there is no evidence that the information was available or relevant.”*

The surviving RCAHMW material demonstrates that professional
historic-building recording existed well before the 1988 decision.

I therefore ask Cadw to address specifically whether that material was
available to Cadw through the inter-agency heritage system at the time and,
if so, what can now be established about its availability.
3. Cadw's own evidence that listing was actively being considered in 1988

The surviving contemporary material indicates that in December 1988 Cadw
was actively considering emergency protection/spot-listing of Great House
Farm, including inspection and consultation concerning the building's
historic significance.

That is important because it demonstrates that this was not retrospectively
invented as a heritage issue decades later. Cadw itself was considering
protection immediately before the building was demolished.

Cadw's present position is that the historical listing file no longer
survives and that its retention arrangements at the time cannot now be
established with certainty.

I am not asking Cadw to speculate about what a destroyed file contained.

I am asking Cadw to distinguish clearly between:

   - what the surviving evidence positively establishes;
   - what information was demonstrably available by 1988;
   - what actions by Cadw in 1988 can still be established;
   - what cannot now be established because the historic record has been
   lost; and
   - any conclusions Cadw considers cannot responsibly be drawn.

That distinction is particularly important when assessing whether the
surviving record provides a sufficiently reliable account of what happened.
4. The planning authority and temporary protection

I also wish to clarify the position concerning temporary protection.

I am not suggesting that Cadw itself necessarily possessed the statutory
power to serve a Building Preservation Notice. I understand that such
protection was a matter for the relevant local planning authority under the
legislation then in force.

The question for Cadw is therefore whether, during the 1988
consideration, *Cadw
advised, discussed or communicated with the relevant planning authority
concerning any available temporary protection mechanism or the need to
prevent demolition pending consideration of listing.*

If Cadw cannot establish what was discussed because the records no longer
survive, that should be stated expressly.
5. The later description of Great House Farm as “a listed building”

I have also identified later archaeological/planning documentation in which
the former site is described in terms including:

“The site formerly contained Great House Farm (a listed building).”

I am not asserting that this wording conclusively proves that Great House
Farm was formally listed at that time.

I am asking Cadw to explain, insofar as the surviving evidence permits,
whether there is any known provenance for that description and whether Cadw
considers it accurate, erroneous, or simply impossible now to determine.

This is relevant because it illustrates the existence of potentially
conflicting historical accounts concerning the building's protection status.
6. The significance of the loss of the 1988 record

Cadw has understandably stated that the historic file cannot now be
produced.

However, the loss of that file creates a historical evidential limitation;
it should not automatically resolve questions arising from the surviving
evidence in Cadw's favour.

The appropriate conclusion may simply be that some aspects of the 1988
decision *cannot now be reconstructed with certainty*.

I would therefore like Cadw to consider whether its previous responses have
drawn that distinction sufficiently clearly.
7. What I am asking Cadw to do

I am asking Cadw to treat this as a formal complaint and provide a
substantive response addressing the following:

*A.* Whether the newly identified 1982 GGAT evidence materially changes
Cadw's understanding of the information environment surrounding Ty Maw Farm
before the 1988 demolition.

*B.* Whether Cadw can establish that the 1974 RCAHMW survey was available
to it in 1988.

*C.* Whether Cadw can establish what archaeological, planning and
historic-building information was available to its officers when the
building was being considered for protection.

*D.* What can now be established about Cadw's communications with the local
planning authority and other heritage bodies during the 1988 listing
consideration.

*E.* Whether temporary protection was discussed or advised upon and, if not
capable of being established, whether Cadw will state that plainly.

*F.* What can be established about the inspection of Great House Farm and
the ultimate listing decision.

*G.* Whether Cadw accepts that the loss of the historic file means that
some aspects of the 1988 decision can no longer be reconstructed reliably.

*H.* Whether Cadw considers the surviving documentary evidence, including
the 1974 survey and 1982 archaeological/planning evidence, should be
reflected in any relevant contemporary heritage record or historical
account.

*I.* Whether Cadw can explain the provenance, insofar as it is capable of
doing so, of the later description of the former site as containing “a
listed building.”

*J.* Whether Cadw considers that its previous responses have adequately
distinguished between the absence of surviving evidence and evidence that
something did not happen.
8. Scope of this complaint

I want to be clear that I am not asking Cadw to determine my family's wider
property or title claims, nor am I asking Cadw to reach a predetermined
conclusion about the historical ownership of the land.

Those matters are separate.

This complaint is confined to *Cadw's own heritage-related role, the 1988
protection/listing process, the information that can now be established as
having existed, and the adequacy and accuracy of Cadw's present explanation
of that history.*

I am also not asking Cadw to speculate about missing documents. On the

I regard that as a proportionate and reasonable opportunity for Cadw to

Haidee,

Thanks.

I am also asking the Senedd to consider whether the circumstances
surrounding the demolition of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth,
and the subsequent planning and heritage history of the site warrant
independent scrutiny and, ultimately, a public inquiry or Senedd committee
inquiry.

I am not asking the Senedd to determine a private property dispute or to
decide legal questions that properly belong before the courts. My concern
is the conduct, decision-making, record-keeping and accountability of
public bodies responsible for heritage protection, planning and local
government.

The surviving evidence presents a series of unusually important questions.

Great House Farm was professionally surveyed by the Royal Commission on the
Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales in 1974. In December 1988, Cadw
was considering the building for emergency spot-listing, with a
contemporary report stating that inspectors were due to visit and consider
the case. The European Commission of Human Rights records that the
Convention application had been introduced on 3 May 1988; BP obtained
possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and
the application was not registered by the Commission until 12 December 1988.

The evidence therefore establishes a very compressed sequence in which
emergency heritage protection was being considered, domestic interim relief
was refused, possession was obtained and the building was then destroyed
within days.

That chronology does not, by itself, establish coordination, deliberate
suppression or unlawful conduct. It does, however, warrant investigation.

There are several specific questions which I believe require answers from
an authority independent of the present local authority:

   1.

   What information and records were actually considered by Cadw when the
   1988 spot-listing decision was made?
   2.

   Was the 1974 RCAHMW architectural survey considered, and if not, why not?
   3.

   What communications took place between Cadw, South Glamorgan County
   Council, BP Properties Ltd, the courts and any other public bodies during
   the critical period immediately preceding demolition?
   4.

   What consideration was given by the local planning authority to the
   available statutory powers of preservation in circumstances where
   demolition was imminent?
   5.

   Why was the building destroyed before there could be an independent
   retrospective architectural examination of the fabric?
   6.

   How should the later archaeological evidence, including the discovery of
   approximately 1,026 burials in 1994, be understood in assessing the
   historic significance of the site and the adequacy of the earlier
   decision-making? I recognise that this later discovery cannot
   retrospectively prove that the 1988 listing decision was unlawful.
   7.

   A 1989 planning document appears to describe the site as having formerly
   contained Great House Farm “(a listed building)”. I ask that this apparent
   discrepancy be investigated and reconciled with the 1988 Cadw decision.
   8.

   What records relating to these decisions still exist, where are they
   held, and have reasonable steps been taken to preserve and disclose them?

I am particularly concerned that the destruction of the physical building
in December 1988 permanently removed primary architectural evidence which
could otherwise have been examined independently.

I also ask the Senedd to consider the wider public-interest question:
whether the present mechanisms for accountability are adequate where a
historic building is destroyed during a period of rapidly developing legal,
planning and heritage proceedings and significant questions remain about
what information was available to decision-makers.

I would therefore ask the Petitions Committee to consider accepting a
petition on this subject and, where appropriate, referring the matter to
the relevant Senedd committee or committees for investigation. I would also
welcome consideration of whether an independent public inquiry, committee
inquiry or other form of external investigation would be appropriate.

I am prepared to provide the underlying documents, chronology, court
material, heritage records, planning documents and correspondence
supporting these questions.

I am not asking the Senedd to adopt my conclusions. I am asking that the
evidence and unanswered questions be examined independently and that the
relevant public bodies be required to account for what they did, what they
knew, and what records exist.

Please confirm the appropriate route for submitting this formally to the
Senedd and whether the material can be referred to the Petitions Committee
for consideration.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

> scrutinising the administration and accountability of Welsh Government and
> associated public bodies, even if the Committee cannot itself determine
> whether the 1988 decision was correct.

>    2. Why do the assessment report, reasons, site notes and consultation
>    records no longer survive?
>    3. Were the records destroyed under an applicable retention policy or
>    other authority, and were they considered for transfer to the appropriate
>    archival institution?
>    4. Is the present position consistent with Welsh Government/Cadw
>    expectations for the preservation of records concerning significant
>    heritage decisions?
>    5. Are current arrangements sufficient to ensure that comparable
>    heritage assessments, particularly where a building is under imminent
>    threat of demolition, are properly documented and retained?

> of either party to the original dispute. They concern *administrative
> practice, institutional record-keeping and the ability of the Senedd and

Royal Commission,

I am researching the demolition of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth, in December 1988 (HER reference GGAT02038s / ST 1681 7331).

I am seeking to establish whether the Royal Commission was consulted or notified before the farmhouse was demolished.

Contemporary reports from 3 December 1988 state that Cadw was considering emergency protection/listing of Great House Farm and that a Cadw inspection was being arranged, including discussion with the Royal Commission for Ancient and Historical Monuments.

The farmhouse was then demolished on 6 December 1988.

I understand that the statutory framework at the time included provisions concerning the recording of historic buildings before authorised demolition. I would therefore be grateful if you could check your records and confirm:

  1.  Whether the Royal Commission received any notification, consultation, referral or request for advice concerning Great House Farm before its demolition in December 1988.
  2.  Whether the Royal Commission was asked to inspect, photograph, record or otherwise document the building before demolition.
  3.  Whether any correspondence exists between the Royal Commission, Cadw, the local planning authority, BP Properties Ltd, or their representatives concerning the proposed demolition.
  4.  Whether the Royal Commission was given an opportunity to complete or supplement its earlier recording of the farmhouse before demolition.
  5.  Whether your records contain any photographs, measured drawings, reports, field notes or other documentation relating specifically to the farmhouse immediately before its demolition.
  6.  If records exist, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers and, where possible, copies.

For context, the Royal Commission had already recorded Great House Farm architecturally in 1974. Contemporary material indicates that the building was subsequently under consideration for emergency listing shortly before its destruction.

There is also an important chronology concerning the occupation and possession of the property: my late father William Buckler had lodged European Commission of Human Rights application 14464/88 on 3 May 1988; BP obtained possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and the Strasbourg application was registered on 12 December 1988.

I am not asking the Royal Commission to express an opinion on the ownership dispute or the legality of the demolition. I am simply seeking to establish, from your records, whether the Commission was notified or consulted and what opportunity, if any, it was given to record the building (our home since 1667) before it was destroyed?

Given the historical and archaeological significance subsequently identified at the site, I would particularly appreciate confirmation of whether any pre-demolition recording was requested or undertaken.

Regards

Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's Dear Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's handling of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth,
particularly the circumstances surrounding its demolition in December 1988
and the subsequent planning process.


Please register this as a formal complaint under the Council's corporate
complaints procedure and provide me with a complaint reference number.


This complaint concerns the Council's administration and exercise of its
planning and heritage responsibilities. It is not intended to constitute an
appeal against a properly made historic planning decision.


1. Great House Farm, Llandough (Cardiff not Cowbridge) was recognised as a
building of historic importance


The planning and archaeological documentation concerning the site
identifies Great House Farm as a building of heritage significance.


In particular, the archaeological material identifies the former building
as a "county treasure" associated with SMR 2038s, while earlier
architectural recording by RCAHMW describes a substantial historic
farmhouse with surviving historic fabric.


The later 1990 archaeological assessment states:


«"Owing to an ownership dispute and the subsequent sudden destruction of
the property in 1988 the building was incompletely understood."»


I regard that statement as highly significant because it records,
contemporaneously with the subsequent planning process, that the building
had been destroyed suddenly and that its archaeological and architectural
history had therefore not been adequately understood or recorded.


2. The Council's apparent failure to take protective action before the 1988
demolition


I ask the Council to investigate what action, if any, its planning and
heritage officers took when Great House Farm was at risk of demolition.


In particular, I ask the Council to establish:


1. Whether the Council knew that Great House Farm was at risk of demolition
before December 1988.

2. Whether the Council received any notification, complaint, application,
correspondence or other warning concerning the proposed demolition.

3. Whether the building had been considered for statutory listing or other
statutory protection.

4. Whether consideration was given to the use of a Building Preservation
Notice or any other available statutory or administrative mechanism capable
of preventing or delaying demolition pending assessment.

5. Whether the Council's heritage officers, planning officers or
archaeological advisers were consulted.

6. Whether any inspection or photographic/architectural record was
undertaken immediately before or after the demolition.

7. Why, given the building's recognised historic significance, the Council
did not secure a comprehensive standing-building record before the building
was lost.


I am not asserting at this stage that a particular statutory power
necessarily had to be exercised. I am asking the Council to investigate
what powers and procedures were available in 1988 and why they were, or

Dear NMR / RCAHMW cataloguing team,

Great House (Ty Mawr), Bonvilston – measured drawings, copies of historic maps, photographic material description and location plan received in the course of Emergency Recording case RCS2/1/1777, filed in nprn order.

There are two distinct Vale of Glamorgan sites with that name:

Regards,

Sion Buckler

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for information about Llandough Primary School and your further enquires around whom you within the Information Governance team you have been corresponding with.

You asked

Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, where applicable, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004, I request copies of records relating to the acquisition of the land used for the construction of Llandough Primary School.

Specifically, I request:

■ The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land.

■ The purchase price or consideration paid for the land.

■ If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis for that arrangement.

■ Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition.

■ Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP (or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company) concerning the transfer of the land.

■ Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition.

■ Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer.

If any of the requested information is already publicly available, please provide the relevant links or document references.

You then issued further correspondence requesting:

On 14 July 2026 you acknowledged my FOI/EIR request (Case Ref 00211027) concerning the acquisition of land for Llandough Primary School.

I replied the same day asking for the name of the officer who sent the acknowledgement. I have received no further response or substantive reply.

Our Response

The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land
The Council holds a conveyance dated 11 June 1965 made between:
1.            Lakeside and Llandough Development Company Limited;
2.            Western Ground Rents Limited; and
3.            The Glamorgan County Council.
A scanned copy of the conveyance and its plan is attached (“the 1965 Conveyance”).

The purchase price or consideration paid for the land
The consideration recorded in the 1965 Conveyance is £16,800.

If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis of that arrangement
The 1965 Conveyance records a purchase for £16,800. No record has been located within the papers held by Legal Services indicating that the land was gifted or transferred at nominal value or below market value.

Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition
Searches were undertaken with Legal Services and Estates Department. No valuation report relating to the acquisition has been identified. The Council does not hold any valuation report falling within the scope of this request.

Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP, or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company, concerning the transfer
No agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company relating to the acquisition of the land have been identified.

Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition
The Council has not identified any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports within its current records management systems which fall within the scope of your request. Given the age of the acquisition, any surviving historic records may have been transferred to Glamorgan Archives. You may wish to contact Glamorgan Archives directly regarding records from this period.

Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer
No planning agreement or planning obligation connected with the 1965 Conveyance has been identified within the title deeds held by Legal Services or, within the Planning Departments records.

We have considered this aspect of your correspondence under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.
The Council’s Information Governance Team deal with requests on a collective basis and all requests will be considered by different officers. The requests are dealt with via a generic e-mail account so that all officers in the Team can consider correspondence.  There are several reasons why the Information Governance Team work in this way.  One reason is to ensure that correspondence is considered as soon as possible and to ensure that messages or e-mails are not sent to individuals and overlooked within our systems overall.  The information requested is also considered to constitute the personal data of a member of staff and disclosure would amount to disclosure to the world at large. Therefore the Council is unable to provide the name of the individual officer, because it is not considered that there is a lawful basis that would make disclosure fair or necessary in the circumstances.  The Council's correspondence is issued on behalf of the authority, and requests for information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 or the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 are made to the Council as a public authority rather than to individual officers. It is not necessary to know the identity of a particular officer in order to submit a valid request for information.

Sirs/Ma'am,

I have been liaising a lot with local authorities in South Wales the last
year regarding my interest in Llandough.

This is a line of enquiry I wish to open about a separate matter. I am
writing on behalf of a US-based company to explore the possibility of
establishing a unique satellite office in South Wales.

The interest is in discussing a potential Commercial Guardianship Tenancy
or alternative lease arrangement for Lavernock Battery and Fort.

I understand that management and ownership of the site involve multiple
stakeholders, and I am reaching out to gauge your initial interest in such
an arrangement.

This proposal is a scenario that solves a common issue for this heritage
and coastal site—preventing dereliction, vandalism, and weathering through
active, professional occupation.

## Why a Commercial Guardianship?
Rather than a traditional commercial takeover, the type of agreement would
have a responsible custodians on site. Guardianship tenancies are not new
to Councils in Wales.

Occupancy would provide:

* Active Security & Maintenance: A regular physical presence on-site to
deter anti-social behavior and immediately flag structural or environmental
issues.

* Preservation of Heritage: respect the Scheduled Ancient Monument status
of the structures. Any workspace configuration would be entirely
low-impact, fully reversible, and designed to protect the historical
integrity of the architecture.

* Sympathetic Integration: mindful of the surrounding Lavernock Point
Nature Reserve and local businesses. Small team to operate quietly,
ensuring zero disruption to local wildlife, public footpaths, or
neighboring holiday operations.

I believe that breathing new life into these historic structures through a
controlled, professional occupancy could be an excellent model for

National Monuments Record / FOI Officer,

This is a request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, so far as the records concern the historic environment, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

I request copies of recorded information held by RCAHMW / the National Monuments Record of Wales relating to a reported discovery of ironwork or “armour” under the rear wing of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan (approx. ST 1681 7331; SMR / HER GGAT02038s; NMR NPRN associated with Great House Farm).

The published citations which identify RCAHMW as the source, and which state that the objects are at the National Museum of Wales, are:

1. RCAHMW, December 1988 — “Unpublished Records relating to Great House Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.” This is the source cited in the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust assessment lodged on planning application 89/01396/OUT (and carried into 92/00671/RES):

   “it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW 1988).”

   Bibliography: RCAHMW 1988 = Unpublished Records relating to Great House Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.
   (GGAT, Land at Great House Farm, Llandough: An Archaeological Assessment, August 1990.)

2. The same statement is repeated in Holbrook & Thomas, “An Early-medieval Monastic Cemetery at Llandough, Glamorgan”, Medieval Archaeology 49 (2005), p. 70 n. 142:

   “Mention should also be made of the fact that medieval ironwork was discovered under the rear wing of Great House Farm c. 1880. It is now in the collections of the National Museums & Galleries of Wales.”

3. The Heneb / Archwilio HER entry for Great House Farm (GGAT02038s) records armour / medieval ironwork found under the rear-wing floor c.1880 and attributes the note to RCAHMW.

Please therefore provide:

A. The full text of R F Suggett’s December 1988 unpublished records relating to Great House Farm, including every page or card that mentions ironwork, armour, a visor, a lance, a helmet, a burial, a soldier, a horse, a museum, or a find under the floor or rear wing / dairy.

B. Any earlier NMR / RCAHMW survey notes, correspondence or drawings that Suggett was using (including H. J. Thomas’s 1974 survey of the house, updated December 1988), insofar as they mention the c.1880 find or the destination of the objects.

C. Any record of the source of Suggett’s statement that the ironwork “is held by the National Museum of Wales” — for example a letter, accession note, conversation record, or museum catalogue reference.

D. Any later NMR / Coflein / correspondence file that confirms, corrects or withdraws that museum attribution.

E. File references, NPRNs and any copy letters sent to or received from the National Museum of Wales / Amgueddfa Cymru, GGAT, Cadw or the Vale of Glamorgan concerning this find.

I am not asking for advice or for a new interpretation. I am asking for the recorded information that underpins the 1988 sentence now cited as fact in the planning file and in Medieval Archaeology.

Please supply electronic copies where held. If any item is already published on Coflein, a catalogue link and reference is enough.

Regards,

Sion Buckler

Dear FOI Team,

Thank you for the internal review outcome dated 8 September 2026.

I note that the review upholds the original decision. I do not, however,
consider that the review has answered the substantive questions raised in
my request for internal review.

I am therefore putting the position on record, while also making a separate
new request for recorded information which your review confirms already
exists.

1. Records identified during the additional searches

On 14 August 2026, Amgueddfa Cymru stated that the additional enquiries had
identified:

"some information relating generally to Great House Farm and the
surrounding area".

The internal review now describes these as:

"a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm,
Llandough".

The wording has therefore changed slightly, but the material fact has not:
the Museum confirms that records referring to Great House Farm were
identified.

My internal-review request specifically asked for those records to be
identified and, where not exempt, provided.

The review does not do so.

Simply stating that the records are considered to fall outside categories 1
to 9 does not identify what they are, where they are held, when they were
created, or their reference numbers.

2. Archived electronic systems

My request of 14 August specifically asked:

- which archived systems were searched;
- the approximate date ranges covered;
- whether historical email or correspondence archives were searched;
- whether legacy collections-management databases were searched; and
- whether any archived systems were unavailable, incomplete or incapable of
being searched.

The review answers none of these questions individually.

Instead, it states:

"archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information
within scope were considered"

and:

"Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing
Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent
solution, and therefore included in the search."

The first statement describes a conclusion, rather than identifying the
systems actually searched.

The second is an assumption about migration completeness. "Would have been
migrated" is not a search result and does not establish that the relevant
historical data was in fact migrated, completely migrated, retained,
searchable and included in the particular search undertaken.

3. Correspondence independent of accessioned objects

This is the most significant issue.

The original request expressly sought correspondence and administrative
records concerning, among other things:

- identification;
- recovery;
- ownership;
- location;
- the Buckler and Williams families;
- Cardiff Council;
- Cardiff Castle;
- the Bute Estate;
- museums; and
- other public authorities.

Those categories were deliberately not restricted to objects which had
subsequently been accessioned by the Museum.

The review states:

"As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum,
no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related
correspondence concerning such objects was identified."

That reasoning addresses correspondence attached to an identified
accessioned object. It does not establish that correspondence was searched
for independently of an accession record.

For example, an enquiry concerning an item, a communication about possible
provenance, a request to identify an object, a discussion concerning
temporary custody, a disposal enquiry, a communication with another
institution, or correspondence about the contents of a property could exist
without the item ever becoming an accessioned Museum object.

Accordingly, the fact that no accessioned object was identified does not
itself establish that no such correspondence existed or was held.

The subsequent statement:

"The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence
concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great
House Farm furniture or household effects."

still does not establish whether the relevant correspondence repositories
were actually searched.

4. Search terms

My internal-review request set out specific terms and variants and asked
the Museum to confirm whether those terms had been used.

The review now states only:

"appropriate search terms and variants were used"

and refers generally to:

"location names, property names, family names and associated variants".

That does not confirm whether the specific terms identified in my request
were searched.

In particular, the review does not say whether searches included
combinations or variants involving:

"Bute Estate", "Bute", "Cardiff Castle", "Cardiff Council", "household
effects", "contents", "dispersal", "recovery", "transfer", "demolition",
"provenance", "ownership"

and the other terms specifically identified in my 14 August correspondence.

The distinction matters because a search for a property name or family name
is not necessarily equivalent to a search for correspondence concerning the
dispersal, recovery, transfer or ownership of its contents.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction

My request also asked what evidential basis existed for the earlier
statement that the Museum was not aware of relevant records having been
transferred to another institution or destroyed.

The review now says:

"The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been
transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken
and the knowledge of relevant collections staff."

This combines two different things: documentary searches and institutional
recollection.

It does not tell me whether the Museum searched:

- transfer or accession-out records;
- disposal records;
- retention and destruction records;
- archival transfer documentation; or
- other records capable of establishing whether material had previously
been transferred or destroyed.

There is an important distinction between:

"no record of transfer or destruction was identified in the records
searched"

and:

"there is no evidence that any transfer or destruction occurred".

The review does not make that distinction sufficiently clear.

6. Searches concerning external institutions

The original request expressly contemplated records concerning Cardiff
Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other external bodies.

The review states:

"Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records."

That is helpful, but it still does not identify what non-catalogue
repositories were searched.

For example, it does not identify whether searches were made of curator
correspondence, departmental files, donor correspondence,
acquisition/disposal correspondence, provenance files, loan files,
institutional correspondence indexes, or other historical administrative
records in which communications with external institutions might have been
recorded.

Again, the issue is not whether the Museum considers the search reasonable.
It is whether the relevant classes of records were actually searched.

7. The significance of the "balance of probabilities" conclusion

I note the review's conclusion that, "on the balance of probabilities", the
Museum does not hold recorded information within the scope of the request.

I do not dispute that a negative FOI determination may ultimately be
reached on that basis.

However, the balance-of-probabilities conclusion necessarily depends upon
the quality, scope and rigour of the searches on which it is based. The
ICO's guidance states that, where a requester disputes whether relevant
information has been located, the authority should be able to provide a
reasoned and detailed account of how it determined that further information
was not held, including the areas searched, staff consulted and, for
electronic searches, the keywords, accounts and time parameters used.

My concern remains that the review repeatedly substitutes statements such
as "we are satisfied", "appropriate", "reasonably capable" and "on the
balance of probabilities" for the underlying factual information about what
was actually searched.

I therefore consider the review outcome insufficiently informative on the
specific search methodology raised in my review request.

I reserve my right to refer the handling of FOI 2026-020 and the internal
review to the Information Commissioner's Office.

Separate new FOI request

Separately from the above, I am now making a new request under the Freedom
of Information Act 2000.

This new request is deliberately limited to recorded information which your
own correspondence confirms was identified or generated in connection with
the searches already undertaken.

Please provide:

A. Records identified

The "small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm,
Llandough" identified during the additional enquiries referred to in your
email of 14 August 2026 and the internal review outcome of 8 September 2026.

For each record, please provide, where recorded:

- title or description;
- date;
- collection, series or department;
- system or repository;
- reference, accession or record number; and
- a copy of the record, subject to any applicable exemption.

If any part of a record is exempt, please identify the exemption relied
upon and provide the remainder where reasonably practicable.

Limb A is confined to the records your 14 August and 8 September letters
say were identified in the FOI 2026-020 additional enquiries. It is not a
new collection-wide search. If any of those records are also in scope of
FOI 2026-032 or FOI 2026-036, please schedule them once and cross-refer.
Please do not refuse this request as a duplicate.

B. Existing search records

Any recorded information already held concerning the searches undertaken
for FOI 2026-020 or its internal review, including any existing:

- search notes;
- search logs;
- search checklists;
- system lists;
- search-term lists;
- IT tickets or instructions;
- archived-system enquiries;
- staff search records; or
- other contemporaneous records documenting the searches undertaken.

I am asking only for recorded information already held. I am not asking the
Museum to create a new narrative or retrospective report.

If no such search records are held, please state that expressly.

Please register this as a new FOI request and provide it with its own
reference number. It is not a further internal review of FOI 2026-020, nor
is it a request to reopen or amend FOI 2026-032 or FOI 2026-036.

I would therefore be grateful if this request could be processed separately
and not treated as a clarification or continuation of those matters.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

shifting the title “Ty Mawr” from the land parcel to the east onto our land
parcel. And appending “Farm” to the descriptor. Making our parcel better
fit the defective title chain being forged, in lieu of my nan’s missing
title chain. The 133 houses they are seeking to build on that land parcel,
ours (now Church View Close) was merged into, is defective. The title chain

Knight Sir Herbert to the Vaughan family in the 1500s. It is even possible
we have been playing the role of virtual freeholder on our land parcel, or
even tenant on the land east of ours. When all things considered, like the
fact we occupied the manorial house since 1667, may even make it possible
that we were and still are the rightful freeholders of Llandough Town
(formerly Cedwyn Estate), with 640 years left on that freehold. Because
Bute’s purchase of the last Vaughan heirs’ estate reportedly did not
include our Ty Mawr.

And Ty Mawr (alias Cefin (a possible attempt at Cedwyn) according to an

all may be a lot bigger and run a lot deeper than even what I am bringing

Vaughan, and so it is not just title, estate and deeds. I only focus on the
parcel we own, for which possession was awarded to BP, to begin unravelling
truths long suppressed and concealed.

In 1974 an ownership hearing did occur to adjudicate the ownership dispute,
but seeing as my nan could not present her title as it was stolen, the
hearing was adjourned. BP then tried to enforce the 1962 possession order.

So in summary: July 1974 = possession case, adjourned, never finally
decided.

September 1974 = old 1962 possession order revived.

October/November 1974 = threatened eviction stopped and warrant withdrawn.
Not licence letters, quashed hearing, but in fact because of overwhelming
court clerk, press and public support.

Another dimension of this, of which there are many, including BP Bailiffs
being undercover soldiers and/or accompanied by soldiers, allegedly even
SAS, is the abrupt demolition of our 800-year-old “county treasure” home.
4am the morning after, almost simultaneously, CADW refused to spot-list it
as Grade II, the council refused to issue a demolition stop order and our

This surely should not have happened prior to the appeal procedure of those

warfare professional, but because other evidence supports it (including
recently declassified ITV coverage which may not even have aired). Along

Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough – Version 5.0.0 (August 2026).

I also enclose a mock application to an AI-assisted mock Chancery Court I
am working with. I have been using iterative research and legal-analysis
processes to test and refine the arguments arising from the historical
evidence, pending any formal legal proceedings on behalf of my family. I
include it not as a substitute for legal proceedings, but to give your
Office the wider context in which I am examining what happened. And an
illustration of a final single legal case which articulates my family’s
grievances. If they were not all so terrified to speak out, still now, even
after 38 years.

The CADW Forensic Critique is deliberately evidence-led. It distinguishes
between established facts, reasonable inferences and matters which cannot
presently be established because the underlying records no longer appear to
be available.

Its central concern is straightforward:

Cadw cannot presently produce sufficient surviving evidence to explain how
its December 1988 decision was reached, nor can it presently explain what
happened to the records documenting that decision.

Albeit we are still corresponding to establish the facts. In any case what
has been established thus far is particularly troubling given what happened
immediately afterwards.

In 1988, Cadw publicly stated that it was considering an appeal to the
Secretary of State for Wales to protect the building. The South Wales Echo
reported on 3 December 1988 that an inspector would visit “this weekend”
and liaise with RCAHMW.

The building was then demolished overnight on 5/6 December 1988, within
hours of the refusal and the simultaneous dismissal of a High Court
injunction.

I am therefore asking your Office to help, at the very least in this
correspondence with CADW, to establish as precisely as possible what
happened.

1. Contact between Cadw and the Welsh Office / Secretary of State

Please confirm, deny or clarify each of the following:

Whether any communication or outreach took place between Cadw, or its
predecessor functions, and the Office of the Secretary of State for Wales /
Welsh Office concerning Great House Farm during the period July–December
1988.

Whether any recommendation, briefing, submission, notification or formal
appeal concerning the protection or listing of Great House Farm was
submitted to the Secretary of State.

Whether my family, as the occupiers and asserted owners of the property,
was ever consulted, contacted or notified by Cadw or the Welsh Office
before the refusal decision of 5 December 1988.

If such communications occurred, I ask that the surviving records be
identified and disclosed.

If they did not occur, I ask that this be stated clearly.

2. What happened to the 1988 assessment records?

Cadw’s responses, including FOI ATISN 27021, the response from Amy Longford
dated 10 July 2026, the subsequent internal review, and the response from
Dr Andy Wigley dated 27 August 2026, indicate that:

only the two July 1988 photographs have been located;

no assessment file, inspector’s notes, decision record or internal
correspondence has been located;

no destruction record, transfer list, accession record or archive schedule
has been located; and

Cadw has stated that unsuccessful listing assessments were historically
retained for approximately three years before transfer or destruction under
the Public Records Act 1958.

This raises an obvious question which I hope your Office will appreciate is
important to my family:

If the records were destroyed, transferred or otherwise disposed of, where
is the record showing that this happened and under whose authority?

I therefore request the immediate production of any surviving destruction,
disposal, transfer or accession documentation relating to the Great House
Farm 1988 assessment file, including certificates, dockets, lists, database
entries, retention schedules, disposal authorities or other contemporaneous
records held by the Welsh Office, its predecessors, Cadw, or any repository
to which relevant records were transferred.

Where such a record exists, please provide its exact wording and identify,
insofar as recorded:

the file reference;

the disposal or transfer authority;

the date of the action;

the relevant retention period;

and the officer or authority responsible for authorising it.

If any residual material remains in existence, I ask that it be preserved
immediately and not destroyed, transferred or otherwise disposed of while
these matters remain under examination.

If no destruction, disposal or transfer documentation exists, I ask that
your Office confirm that expressly.

3. The unanswered questions surrounding the decision itself

I also ask your Office to address, or to require Cadw to address, the
outstanding questions identified in Part XII of the accompanying Forensic
Critique.

In particular:

Who was the decision-maker responsible for the refusal on 5 December 1988?

What was the registered file reference, title and record series?

What evidence was actually considered?

Was the 1974 RCAHMW survey (ST 16817331) considered?

Were SMR 2038/2038s and the relevant 1978–1980 GGAT reports considered?

What was the basis, authorship and status of the July 1988 “YYY” coding?

What communications took place with BP Properties or its agents, the local
planning authority, RCAHMW, GGAT or the High Court during the critical
period?

Was a Building Preservation Notice considered?

What retention and disposal schedule applied to the assessment?

What was the scheduled disposal/review date?

Who authorised disposal, if disposal occurred?

Which repositories and catalogues have been searched, including The
National Archives and historic Welsh Office records?

Do comparable unsuccessful listing assessments from 1988–1991 survive, and
if so, how were they retained?



These are not questions I ask simply because I disagree with the historical
decision.



I am trying to establish what evidence was before the decision-maker, what
process was followed, and what happened to the official record afterwards.

That distinction matters.



4. Independent verification

I therefore ask your Office to confirm whether it has searched, or will now
search, The National Archives catalogue and relevant historic Welsh Office
transfer documentation for records concerning Great House Farm.

If this has not already been done comprehensively, I ask that it be
undertaken and that Cadw be asked to undertake any corresponding searches
necessary to establish whether the missing assessment material was ever
transferred elsewhere.

I would also ask that any surviving records relating to the case be
preserved while these enquiries are ongoing.

5. Why I am asking

I appreciate that this is a historic matter.

But for my family it is not simply history.

This was our home. It was the place into which I was born, and the
destruction of the building came at the end of a much longer dispute
concerning our family’s occupation, land and property rights.

I have spent considerable time reconstructing what happened from surviving
court records, land records, archaeological evidence, newspapers, archival
material, FOI responses and contemporary documentation. I am not asking
your Office to accept every conclusion I have drawn.

I am asking for something more fundamental:

where the Government and its agencies can still establish what happened, I
ask that they do so; where the evidence no longer exists, I ask that they
say so plainly; and where the record of its disappearance should exist, I
ask that it be identified.

My family has lived with the consequences of these events for decades. I
believe that, at this stage, the least that can reasonably be expected is
openness, proper record-keeping and an honest examination of what happened.

I therefore ask that this correspondence, together with the attached CADW —
Forensic Critique v5.0.0, be treated as a formal request for recorded
information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, as well as a request
for clarification of the records-management position concerning Cadw and
the historic Welsh Office functions now falling within the responsibility
of your Office.

I would be grateful for a substantive response addressing each of the
matters above individually.

Yours sincerely,



Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sergeant)

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for an internal review of FOI 2026-020 concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

The reviewer has considered your original request, the responses provided by the Museum, the additional enquiries undertaken following your request for clarification on 3rd August 2026, and the concerns raised in your email requesting an internal review.

We are satisfied that the request was interpreted correctly and that reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken to identify information falling within the scope of the request. Following the original response, the Museum undertook additional enquiries across relevant collections records and archived electronic records in order to satisfy itself that no information had been overlooked.

We are satisfied that the searches undertaken were appropriate to the nature and scope of the request and that no further searches are required in order to determine whether Amgueddfa Cymru holds information within scope.  The review therefore upholds the original decision that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough falling within categories 1 to 9 of your request.

Response to the points raised

1. Information identified concerning Great House Farm
During the additional enquiries, a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm, Llandough were identified. These records do not relate to furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm and do not fall within categories 1 to 9 of your original request. The reviewer is therefore satisfied that they fall outside the scope of the request.

2. Scope of the archived electronic search

We are satisfied that archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information within scope were considered as part of the searches undertaken. Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent solution, and therefore included in the search.

3. Correspondence and administrative records
The review considered whether correspondence or administrative records relating to the requested items were held.

The Museum's collections records include accession documentation and associated collection records relating to objects acquired by the Museum. Searches of those records did not identify any furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm.   As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum, no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related correspondence concerning such objects was identified.

The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great House Farm furniture or household effects.

4. Search terms
We are satisfied that appropriate search terms and variants were used across the relevant collections management systems, collection records and associated documentation. These included relevant location names, property names, family names and associated variants reasonably capable of identifying records within scope.

The review is satisfied that the search methodology was reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction
The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken and the knowledge of relevant collections staff.  The review did not identify any records showing that information within the scope of your request had been transferred to another institution or destroyed.

For clarity, the Museum's position is that no relevant records were identified.

6. Records concerning external institutions
We note that your request sought records concerning communications with Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other bodies regarding objects originating from Great House Farm. Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records. Relevant collection documentation and associated records were also considered.

No records were identified concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms, or other movable property originating from Great House Farm, including correspondence with the organisations referred to in your request.

7. Advice and assistance
The Museum does not hold information identifying a specific department, collection, archive or record series within Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle that is likely to contain the information you seek. The advice previously provided reflected our general view that those organisations would be more likely than Amgueddfa Cymru to hold records relating to the ownership, management or disposal of property associated with Great House Farm.

Conclusion
Having considered all of the information available, we are satisfied that Amgueddfa Cymru undertook reasonable and proportionate searches and that, on the balance of probabilities, the Museum does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of your request. The original decision is therefore upheld.

If you remain dissatisfied, you have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office.



Cofion cynnes,

particular transaction I am trying to establish.

My principal question is *not whether there are deeds between the Bute
Estate and Alfred Thomas*. The key transaction I am trying to locate and
verify is the *1877 transaction concerning Daniel Thomas and the Bute
Estate*, which I understand from the surviving family evidence to have
concerned a defined portion of Great House Farm, including the farmhouse
and surrounding land. I see an 1877 agreement between both parties, for
that year, but for a different property in Cardiff. I wondered if it was
mis labelled and if you could validify its content, particularly any map
data. So as the integrity of the descriptor of the record is assured or
revisited.

The issue is whether the Bute Estate *conveyed, granted or otherwise dealt
with that defined parcel in favour of Daniel Thomas*, and, crucially, what
the instrument and its plan actually show about the boundaries and the
nature of the interest created. In 1877.

This is important because the present documentary reconstruction I am
preparing treats the 1877 instrument as the potential starting point for
the separate House Plot chain. The working case is that the instrument
dealt with the farmhouse land separately from the eastern
agricultural/quarrying parcel, with provisions connected to quarrying and
the subsequent passing of the house land to the occupying Williams family
when quarrying ceased. That proposition is expressly being treated as a
matter requiring verification against the original instrument and plan,
rather than as an established fact.

I therefore wonder whether the catalogue search could be reconsidered
specifically on the following basis:

*Bute Estate → Daniel Thomas → defined land at Llandough / Great House
Farm, approximately 1876–1878*

including instruments which may not themselves be catalogued under “Great
House Farm” or “Daniel Thomas”, but which might appear under:

   - the name of the property or former field name;
   - the Marquess of Bute or his trustees as grantor;
   - Daniel Thomas as builder, quarryman, lime-burner or occupier;
   - a lease, conveyance, agreement, surrender or counterpart;
   - quarrying or mineral rights;
   - a plan accompanying an instrument;
   - or a transaction recorded in a Bute Estate rental, ledger or estate
   correspondence rather than in the deed catalogue.

I appreciate that your catalogue may simply contain no surviving record of
this transaction. If that is the position, that is useful information in
itself. What I am particularly trying to establish is whether *the 1877
transaction has been positively searched for and not found*, as opposed to
there being no later catalogue entry linking Daniel or Alfred Thomas to the
Bute Estate.

item(s) within D696 contain the *book plans and rental books for Western
Ground Rents Ltd c.1938–1944*, particularly anything relating to Great
House Farm, Llandough or the land occupied by John Williams.

This is potentially very relevant because the documentary issue I am
investigating is whether the later WGR estate corresponded geographically
with the parcel dealt with by the Bute Estate in 1877, or instead with the
separate agricultural/quarrying parcel.

Dear Sion Buckler,

Thank you for your email of 22nd August, received into our enquiries system 24th August.

To answer your points in turn:


  1.  DBDT/10/19 describes Daniel Thomas as ‘of the Town of Cardiff, Builder’.  There are no further identifying details for Daniel Thomas in the documents.  We can provide copies of the documents at a charge or they can be accessed for free in our public searchroom.  Please let us know if you would like a quote for digital copies.
  2.  There are no additional deeds described on our catalogue between Daniel or Alfred Thomas and the Bute Estate.
  3.  There are no additional records relating to quarrying in Llandough or around Ty Mawr / Great House Farm.
  4.  If you have not already got a copy of Daniel Thomas’ will, you can apply for a copy of probate from the Probate Office: Search probate records for documents and wills (England and Wales) - GOV.UK<https://www.gov.uk/search-will-probate>.
  5.  We think you have probably already covered all the material we have on this matter but…
1-3)  We do not hold the majority of the Bute Estate records.  I attach a finding aid to the Bute Estate records that are currently held by Cardiff Library. These records are soon to be transferred to us so please let us know if there is anything on this list that you are interested in.  Other records of the Bute Estate can be found at the National Library of Wales.
4)  We are not sure if you have consulted D696 which includes a book plans and rental books for land owned by Western Ground Rents Ltd c1938-1944.
6. Have you looked at historic Ordnance Survey plans to show boundaries?  Some of these can be viewed online e.g. Map Finder - with Outlines - National Library of Scotland<https://maps.nls.uk/geo/find/#zoom=15.0&lat=51.44833&lon=-3.19885&layers=101&b=1&z=0&point=51.45192,-3.19801&i=135196558>.  Mary consulted the 1910 Land Valuation book for Llandough (DVAL/1/33) but we do not have the corresponding maps to go with this – you would need to contact the National Archives for a copy of this.

We hope that this information is of use to you.  Please note that we aim to answer all emails in order but the longer more complicated ones may take up to 15 working days to respond to.

Yours sincerely,

Louise Hunt
